#324. How to Intercept HTTP/3 Traffic: QUIC and Qpack

📅 25 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2531 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Interceptsuite

How to Intercept HTTP/3 Traffic: QUIC and Qpack

📅 25 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2531 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Interceptsuite

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, short answer: HTTP/3 does not go through an HTTP proxy, because it runs over QUIC, and QUIC runs over UDP.
  • It has been revealed that in this post we intercept real HTTP/3 traffic from curl and from Microsoft Edge.
  • Industry observers note that this post uses InterceptSuite, so you should know what it is and what it is not.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, short answer: HTTP/3 does not go through an HTTP proxy, because it runs over QUIC, and QUIC runs over UDP. Most HTTP proxies, such as Burp Suite, are built on HTTP over TCP, so they never see it. To intercept HTTP/3 you need a proxy that can relay UDP and can act as a man in the middle for QUIC. After that, the work is about streams and header compression: the request is not text any more, it is bytes on a QUIC stream, compressed with QPACK.

It has been revealed that in this post we intercept real HTTP/3 traffic from curl and from Microsoft Edge. Then we use a small lab server to look at every byte, so the QUIC and QPACK parts are easy to follow.

Industry observers note that this post uses InterceptSuite, so you should know what it is and what it is not. It is not built for HTTP. It is built for raw network traffic: TCP, TLS, UDP, DTLS and QUIC. Because it can intercept UDP and QUIC, it can handle HTTP/3 too. But it does not come with an HTTP parser, and that is also true for HTTP/3. The core reveals raw bytes.

Recent findings suggest that to read and edit those bytes as HTTP, InterceptSuite has an extension API, and there is an official, open source HTTP/3 extension that decodes the QUIC stream and QPACK headers into text. You can read the code, change it, or send a fix. The decoding in the screenshots below comes from that extension, not from the core.

If you have only used HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2, three things are different.

Recent findings suggest that 1. It runs on QUIC, not TCP. HTTP/3 (RFC 9114) is HTTP carried over QUIC (RFC 9000). QUIC packets travel inside UDP datagrams. TLS 1.3 is part of the QUIC handshake (RFC 9001), so there is no separate "TCP then TLS" step.

2. The client has to learn that the server speaks HTTP/3. The ALPN name for HTTP/3 is h3. A server can advertise it with an Alt-Svc response header, and a DNS HTTPS record can advertise it too (RFC 9460). So a browser often makes its first request over TCP, then moves to QUIC.

In a recent development, 3. Everything is a stream. A QUIC connection carries many streams. The two lowest bits of a stream ID tell you what it is (RFC 9000, section 2.1):.

In HTTP/3, every client-started two-way stream is one request and its response (stream 0, 4, 8 and so on). The one-way streams are for housekeeping: a control stream, and two QPACK streams. Their type is the first byte on the stream: 0x00 control, 0x02 QPACK encoder, 0x03 QPACK decoder (RFC 9114, section 6.2 and RFC 9204, section 4.2).

One more detail that matters for interception. The first packets of a QUIC connection (the Initial packets) are protected with keys that anyone can calculate from the connection ID, so they have no real secrecy (RFC 9001, section 5). That is why a passive observer can still see things like the server name in the handshake. Everything after the handshake is encrypted with keys from the TLS 1.3 exchange. You cannot read it without being one of the two ends. A proxy that wants to read HTTP/3 has to be one of the two ends.

HTTP proxies use CONNECT to open a tunnel. In HTTP/3, CONNECT still builds a tunnel to a TCP connection (RFC 9114, section 4.4). To tunnel UDP over HTTP there is a different method, CONNECT-UDP (RFC 9298), and most tools and apps do not use it.

In a recent development, SOCKS5 can relay UDP. The command is UDP ASSOCIATE (RFC 1928). But many clients never use it. For example, the Chromium network docs say that in Chrome, SOCKSv5 is only used to proxy TCP-based requests and cannot relay UDP (Chromium proxy docs). So pointing a browser at a SOCKS5 proxy does not send its QUIC traffic through that proxy, and you are not testing the QUIC path.

That leaves two practical ways to get QUIC traffic into a proxy:.

For how this compares with mitmproxy, see the QUIC interception post.

Open Proxy, then Redirect, click Add, type the program name (for example curl.exe), leave the action on Proxy, and save. Then click Start Redirect. The status line claims Redirecting through the proxy at 127.0.0.1:4444, and the program's TCP and UDP traffic goes through InterceptSuite without changing any setting in the program.

Industry observers note that A rule can also limit the destination hosts and ports. The first matching rule decides, and programs that match no rule are left alone. Remember to trust the InterceptSuite CA on the machine, as in the quick start.

curl is a good first test because it is simple and does exactly what you tell it. It needs a build with HTTP/3 support. This example runs on Windows. The curl that ships with Windows (8.21.0 here) does not support HTTP/3: curl -V does not list HTTP3 in its features. So we installed a second curl build that does:.

The fresh build (8.23.0) lists HTTP3, ngtcp2 and nghttp3 in curl -V. Check yours the same way before you test, and make sure the new curl is the one that runs (open a new terminal after the install).

Recent findings suggest that --http3-only makes curl use HTTP/3 and nothing else, so it cannot quietly fall back to TCP. With the Redirect rule on, curl worked without any proxy option and its output revealed HTTP/3 200. No -k was needed, because curl used the Windows trust store, where the InterceptSuite CA is installed.

In Proxy History the connection appeared as QUIC with host cloudflare-quic.com and ALPN h3:.

The first client packet (46 bytes) is the request. With the HTTP/3 tab it reads like this:.

Now turn Intercept ON, run curl again, and change the request while it is held. Replace user-agent: curl/8.23.0 with user-agent: edited-by-proxy and press Forward:.

According to recent reports, the test site prints back what it saw. The first run notes uag=curl/8.23.0. The run with the edit says:.

So the server got the edited header, and curl never knew. The response is readable too:.

Look at curl's SETTINGS frame, from the client:.

According to recent reports, QPACK_MAX_TABLE_CAPACITY: 0 means curl does not use the QPACK dynamic table at all. That is why every curl request is easy to read and edit. We will see the opposite case later.

Browsers are harder, for two reasons.

The fix is to start the browser with three flags:.

It has been revealed that is the base64 SHA-256 of the CA's public key. You calculate it from your own CA file:.

Industry observers note that edge indicates a bar saying the flag is unsupported. That is expected, and it is why you should use a test profile and not your daily one. Close all Edge windows before you start it, or the flags are ignored.

With the Redirect rule for msedge.exe on, open https://cloudflare-quic.com/. The page states "your browser used HTTP/3":.

According to recent reports, in InterceptSuite the same visit was a QUIC connection with ALPN h3. The request from Edge, decoded by the extension:.

And the response, with the alt-svc: h3=":443" header the site uses to advertise HTTP/3:.

The response body here is content-encoding: gzip. The extension decompresses it for display, so the body reveals as HTML.

Edge's SETTINGS are very different from curl's:.

Sources indicate that edge offers a 64 KB dynamic table and up to 100 blocked streams, so after the first request, Edge can send headers as table references. The QPACK section below explains what that means for reading and editing.

UDP ASSOCIATE works in two parts.

The header, from RFC 1928 section 7:.

The association lives as long as the TCP connection that asked for it. If that TCP connection closes, the UDP association ends (RFC 1928, section 6). This is easy to forget when you write your own client.

Recent findings suggest that interceptSuite listens on 127.0.0.1:4444 for SOCKS5 over TCP and 127.0.0.1:4445 for the UDP relay (see the quick start). The reply to UDP ASSOCIATE points to 127.0.0.1:4445.

Real servers make it hard to see what is going on, so here is a small lab. Both sides use Python and aioquic.

The lab client skips certificate checks. That is fine for a lab. A real app must trust the proxy's CA certificate, or it will close the connection when it sees the forged certificate. See Install the CA certificate for that step.

The lab client sent one request:.

Here is Proxy History after the client connected, sent requests, and closed.

Industry observers note that the host column demonstrates h3.lab.test. That is the server name from the TLS handshake. The ALPN column shows h3. The Protocol column says QUIC.

Industry observers note that the thing most people do not expect is the number of rows. One request gave 10 entries, not 2. Each row is a chunk of data from one QUIC stream, in the order the proxy saw it. The small ones are all HTTP/3 housekeeping:.

The client's control stream is three bytes longer than the server's: 0D 01 08 at the end, which is a MAX_PUSH_ID frame.

According to recent reports, filtering helps a lot here. The filter box understands things like connection_id == 3 and size > 100. The available fields are src_ip, dst_ip, port, direction, protocol, size, modified, connection_id, type, data, host and alpn.

With the HTTP/3 extension loaded, the control stream entry is shown as text:.

According to recent reports, the 50 00 part is a QUIC variable-length integer. The first two bits (01) say it uses two bytes, and the value is 0x1000, which is 4096. This one matters later, because QPACK's dynamic table is off by default. Both QPACK settings default to zero (RFC 9204, section 5). This server turned it on and allowed 16 blocked streams.

Sources indicate that now the request itself. This is the raw view of the held request packet:.

According to recent reports, you can see the body (user=alice&pw=hunter2), because the body is not compressed. The headers are unreadable. This is QPACK. It is HPACK's cousin for HTTP/3 (RFC 9204), and it does three things:.

The HTTP/3 extension from the Extension repository decodes all of this into text. Open the HTTP/3 tab on the same packet:.

Industry observers note that the core of InterceptSuite shows HTTP/3 as raw bytes. The decoded view comes from this extension. The extension is a normal Python file, and you can read it. Its _decode function parses the QUIC variable-length integers, the HTTP/3 frames, then the QPACK block with the static table and Huffman decoder.

According to recent reports, turn Intercept ON. By default it holds client-to-server packets. There is also an Intercept response option for the other direction.

Recent findings suggest that when the client sends its request, the request packet is held and the queue states 1 packet(s) waiting. Change two things in the HTTP/3 tab: the x-demo header and the body.

Sources indicate that then press Forward. The server printed this:.

Recent findings suggest that so the server received the edited request. The client got a normal 200 answer from the server, and its own copy of the request was never changed.

In Proxy History, the row shows Modified: Yes, and the viewer can show the Original and Edited versions:.

Two practical points from doing this:.

The extension does not patch the old bytes. It builds a upcoming HEADERS frame. From the source, the rules are:.

This is the part that needs care. So far everything decoded nicely. Now send more requests on the same connection (same headers, different path) and look again.

The sizes tell the story. Requests 1 and 2 were 122 bytes each. Request 3 was 13 bytes. And at some point, a 114-byte entry indicated up on the client's QPACK encoder stream.

Here are the 13 bytes of request 3, the way they were on the wire:.

Recent findings suggest that where are the entries? In the 114-byte entry on the encoder stream. Its first bytes are C0 88 9D 95 E8 1C 6B A4 A8 4F, which is "insert :authority, with a Huffman-coded value" (the value decodes to h3.lab.test). The client sent the long header values once, and every later request only sends numbers. This is a good design. It is also what makes interception harder.

Look at what the HTTP/3 tab shows for request 3:.

The server's response did the same thing. After a few responses, its header block started using the dynamic table, and the HTTP/3 tab highlights the body but only placeholders for two of the headers:.

There is one more thing to see here. In the capture, the 13-byte request (row 30) arrived before the 114-byte encoder stream entry (row 31). That is allowed by design. QPACK lets a request stream wait ("block") until the inserts it needs have arrived. The server declared it could keep up to 16 blocked streams (the QPACK_BLOCKED_STREAMS setting we saw above). Later a single byte 88 comes back from the server on its decoder stream. That is a Section Acknowledgment for stream 8, which was the third request: the decoder tells the encoder it processed a header block that needed the table (RFC 9204, section 4.4.1).

So two things follow for a tester:.

Right-click a row in Proxy History and choose Send to Replay.

The session opens with the details filled in: host, port, protocol QUIC, ALPN h3, Newly introduced bidirectional stream, and End stream (FIN) ticked. HTTP/3 request streams are client-started two-way streams, so that is the correct choice. The FIN flag matters because the lab server only answers after it sees the end of the request.

In the lab the host name h3.lab.test is only a name in the TLS handshake and does not resolve, so change the host to 127.0.0.1. In the HTTP/3 tab, change the path to /admin and x-demo to replayed, then press Send.

The conversation highlights what happened on the wire:.

The server printed GET /admin x-demo= replayed, and the response JSON reveals "path": "/admin" and "x_demo": "replayed".

If the edited text leaves a broken header block, Replay sends only a few bytes (25 here) and the server closes the connection:.

Sources indicate that 0x106 is H3_FRAME_ERROR. RFC 9114 states that if a stream ends and the last frame on it is cut short, the receiver must treat it as a connection error of this type (RFC 9114, section 7.1). In plain words: the frame header promised more bytes than the stream delivered. If you hand-craft HTTP/3 bytes in the Raw or Hex tab, this is the error you will meet first. It means your frame length does not match your data.

You can find the current list in the protocol compatibility matrix.

Related reading: Replay documentation, Proxy History documentation, the HTTP/3 extension source, and Intercepting QUIC and HTTP/3 when mitmproxy isn't enough.

According to recent reports, you can try all of this on your own server with the 7-day trial. Only test servers you own or are allowed to test.

#323. Rust changed me as a developer

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 18m • 📚 Deep Dive (3559 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Startifact

Rust changed me as a developer

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3559 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Startifact

⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The programming language you use affects how you think as a software developer 1.
  • I've been developing with Rust for over 6 years; more than 4 years professionally now.
  • Industry observers note that what I learned and am going to discuss here is not exclusive to Rust.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The programming language you use affects how you think as a software developer 1. That may seem surprising to you; you may have picked up JavaScript pretty quickly knowing Python, and it didn't really affect how you think or develop. That's because those languages are pretty similar. The more different a programming language is from what you're used to, the more it can change you. Rust was quite different to me, so it did.

I've been developing with Rust for over 6 years; more than 4 years professionally now. One of the reasons I really wanted to become more proficient with Rust is because I knew it would challenge me, and hopefully change me for the better as a developer. I think it did.

Industry observers note that what I learned and am going to discuss here is not exclusive to Rust. You can encounter many of these concepts in other contexts, and indeed I had encountered quite a few of them already. But in this case, Rust helped bring them into better focus.

We're all familiar with product types, though not usually under that name:.

The fields of the Human struct 2 can vary independently from each other, and we have to deal with all possible combinations: all possible first names and last names, combined. The product of their combinations, to to speak.

In a recent development, but it turns out there's another type thing that's been around forever but that the programming community has mostly been been ignoring 3: the sum type. A sum type expresses variants: something is either one thing, or another, out of a bunch of variants:.

A Person is either a human or a cat: that's the sum of the possiblities. Each variant can have data associated with it, and this can be a product type, but the Person type is just these options (two in this case). In code where you need to deal with a person, you need to handle each variant by match in on the object. The Rust compiler enforces this.

In a recent development, when you handle the human variant, you only need to worry about first_name and last_name. You don't have to worry about name or cuteness at all. These cases are distinct from each other.

It turns out that it's really helpful to model stuff using sum types. People using functional programming languages already knew this. You can model optionality (null) this way: you got either some value, or nothing. You can also model errors: it's either okay (with whatever value you return in case of success), or an error (with a value describing the error).

Any language without sum types now feels impoverished to me. I know I can simulate it with some type field, but the job of a programming language is to help me handle basic stuff, and this is basic stuff.

Industry observers note that in an object oriented programming language, you handle variants using dynamic dispatch and an interface (or inheritance). You do this:.

The idea is that you can now use Person anywhere without worrying about the details inside: it's loosely coupled. You only use their interface.

Industry observers note that this is indeed a great idea, but Rust taught me that this has tradeoffs I may not want to pay for. You pay two things: performance, and the need to create the interface.

Let's talk about the need to create the interface. You need to devise an interface that actually makes sense for your application: how are you using humans and cats everywhere? Doing this work of abstraction may be extremely worthwhile to do, especially if you anticipate unknown future persons that you need to be able to plug in later without having to modify the code that uses them -- you want your code use the open/closed principle.

Industry observers note that but what if you are developing a single domain, and inside that you just want to be able to handle cats and humans and that's it? There's just no need to plug in other types of persons, and certainly not from outside.

According to recent reports, or let's say you do want to add a new variant once every while. Say you want to add Dog. Maybe you're actually okay going through the code that handles Human and Cat and add handling for dogs too? Maybe it actually is helpful to see those other handlers right there too when you do so? The compiler is going to ensure you don't miss any spots!

Or what if the abstraction you are trying to devise is the variance and that's more or less what you can say about it? For error handling, the abstraction is either okay with some value, or some error value.

In this case you may be paying the price of creating an interface without it being worthwhile.

Industry observers note that enum may be all you actually need -- low ceremony, and statically checked. Finally I'll note that enums don't lock you out from creating that abstraction - you can add methods to an enum too, just like on a struct.

Enums made me a better programmer as now I have another elementary, simple, easy to understand language construct for abstraction in my mental toolbox.

In many languages there are two types of dispatch: dynamic dispatch, which we've discussed in case of our Person interface, and conditional dispatch, like this:.

According to recent reports, rust has dynamic dispatch, if you ask for it. It also has the powered up version of conditional dispatch I already discussed: match on enums. It has conditional dispatch too - that's just [a special case][https://docs.rs/bool/latest/bool/enum.Boolean.html].

There's another type of dispatch that Rust makes you think about: dispatch that's statically compiled.

In a recent development, what if you're dealing either with groups of humans or groups of cats, and you want to do some operations on them, and those operations have common behavior (say, you want to count them). The group, or collection, doesn't really care about what's in it, as long as every item fulfills certain basic properties.

You could create an enum Person; either an enum or an interface with multiple implementations, and then dispatch during runtime to every member of the group based on whether that entry is a human or a cat. But this means you have to account for mixed groups of humans and cats, even though we just said those don't actually exist.

In a recent development, instead, you can express this differently in Rust. You still have a Person interface (trait), but you compose your individual type of Person (Human or Cat) during compile time.

Rust now refuses to compile if you use non-cat operations on items in the group, That's an invariant you now do not need to worry about anymore. This will be familiar to you with generics in other languages like TypeScript or Python.

In Rust, when you process your group of cats, there is no individual check somewhere whether an entry is a human or a cat, as it already knows it's all cats before the program even ran. Rust directly dispatches to the cat code, and the human code is not play. You avoid indirect dispatch for every group member, which can matter in situations where performance is crucial.

Rust made me a better programmer as I now better understand the connection between dispatch and performance.

It has been revealed that when I discovered Python coming from C++ back in the late 1990s, dynamic typing was a revelation. You could so much with so little ceremony. For the last decade or so I have been on a long winding road back to types (far more ergonomic types) and more ceremony. I have the impression many have been on this journey along with me 4.

Industry observers note that types can statically check your code before it runs. In Rust, they can help the compiler compile stuff down to really high performance code. Both are great. But types can also have more subtle benefits. Let me get into this by analogy.

Obvious: Automated tests ensure various properties of your code work and remain working.

Subtle: Writing tests forces you to think about the architecture and APIs you're implementing more carefully. Making code testable can lead to better architecture. This is the insight of test driven development.

Obvious: People (and now machines) can understand 5 the why and what of your software by reading the documentation.

Sources indicate that subtle: The act of writing the documentation can force you think about the architecture and APIs of your software. If you can't write about it, maybe you haven't gotten it right yet? That's documentation driven development.

According to recent reports, obvious: Statically check your code before it runs! Prevent runtime errors! Performance!

Industry observers note that subtle: You model the domain model using types, trying to make sure it hangs together. Enums are really valuable here. You express parse, don't validate in them. The types guide the architecture and APIs of your software.

Rust brought into focus how types are yet another tool to help me think while I develop.

Rust made me a better programmer as it let me fully embrace type driven development.

According to recent reports, here is the biggest surprise I had coming to Rust. Much of the behavior I associated with dynamic interpreted languages with a rich runtime like Python can actually be done statically in Rust using macros.

Industry observers note that say you want to dump the state of a Python object -- you inspect all its fields, look at their type, turn each into a string, combine all the strings together into a substantial one. Now you can store it somewhere. Later on you restore that string back into an object. You can save and load any objects: magic! Python calls this pickle.

What if you need to serialize to JSON? Python has a type system, and a library like Pydantic inspects the type objects during runtime and then uses this information to let you automatically serialize a Python object to JSON, or parse it back into Python again. More magic!

Industry observers note that rust is a compiled language. Types aren't runtime objects. Without reflection, which takes special effort, runtime introspection of types is not a thing in Rust.

But Rust can still do what Pickle and Pydantic do, at compile time.

Recent findings suggest that with serde, Rust's answer to pickle and Pydantic, you use a normal Rust type, annotate it with a few declarations, and then you can serialize it to JSON, or toml config format, and many other formats, and load it back again. The annotation looks like this:.

In a recent development, with clap, you create the type that expresses exactly what command line arguments you expect (with enums too!), document it using the normal way you document any API in Rust, and boom, you have a CLI with built in help. The code that handles the various cases gets well-typed data - at that point it's been parsed correctly already, using the same type you used to express the CLI.

It has been revealed that again declarative #[] stuff going on. It looks a lot like decorators in Python. But Python decorators are executed during runtime, and we just stated Rust doesn't normally let you do that.

Recent findings suggest that how does that work in Rust? Macros! Macros lets you write code that generates code during compile time. With serde, the macro generates a whole bunch of serialization code and deserialization code for the types annotated with it. This generated code gets compiled along with the rest of your code. The compiler can optimize it just like any other code.

Code generation is scary. Macros are scary. Doing introspection in a dynamically typed language is a lot easier than using Rust macros, where code is parsed and generated. Macros shouldn't be randomly mixed with application code; macros belong in frameworks. That said, something being easy doesn't mean it should be used casually: in Python you typically want to carefully encapsulate your magic in a declarative framework too.

Rust made me a better programmer as I learned about a new class of framework patterns.

According to recent reports, rust famously lets you write code without memory leaks that doesn't use a garbage collector. It also stops you from mutating data you're also reading elsewhere, making it impossible to stumble into whole classes of weird undefined behavior, especially with code that runs in parallel.

Rust's ownership system is one of the main things that makes learning Rust hard. Python, JavaScript, Java and many other languages have mutable references everywhere, and you can just create cyclic data structures. Rust won't let you do either out of the box.

The equivalent of this does not compile in Rust:.

Rust won't just let you have circular references, in this case both children and a parent reference.

Recent findings suggest that this feels very limiting at first! What do you do instead? For mutating stuff, you learn how to separate mutation (often during construction) from using your data. That is a thing that's good to do in many contexts -- less invariants makes it's easier to reason about, but it takes a bit of getting used to Rust strictly enforcing it.

It has been revealed that for circular references it's trickier. I will go into it next, when I discuss arenas.

In a recent development, A weird thing happens: if you lean into this friction it can improve the architecture of your codebase. Code becomes less coupled. It's hard to create weird backchannels with action at a distance that makes code difficult to understand, test and debug 7.

Rust code locally can be difficult to understand. But how the data flows, what does what, in the larger codebase, tends to be cleaner.

Rust made me a better programmer as I now think about ownership more carefully, which has a positive impact on architecture.

Recent findings suggest that A few years ago I analyzed a bunch of XML tree libraries in Rust. The best I found, roxmltrree, has an immutable tree. But I needed a mutable tree. I found quite a few libraries that did support mutability, but many did not support parent references. You couldn't walk up the ancestor chain of a node. This, along with missing support for some XML features, is why I created my own in the form of Xot.

The reason for this surprising lack of parent references is the ownership limitation I discussed before: Rust makes circular references difficult. You can get around it using reference counted types and internal mutability, but in a lot of cases this pattern isn't really optimal -- it's verbose, less performant, and reference count cycles risk memory leaks. What you do instead is store nodes in an array and you use the array indexes to node as your reference. You can then have an index referencing your parent, and use index references to your children, or any other circular reference.

A fancy word for this pattern is an 'arena' and in Rust they show up everywhere.

According to recent reports, in an arena, you store a lot of objects together in the same region of memory (in an array). What does it let you do?

iterate fast over its contents. Objects being in the same memory region means the CPU can use its cache effectively. This is much faster than arbitrary main memory access and loops really benefit.

fast allocation. The arena is allocated from the heap as a block, and after that your allocations may just be a few increments.

interning: you store something once in the arena and use it in many places, so you don't duplicate data.

the arena owns its stuff. Everything in the arena has the same lifetime. Indexes between objects in an arena can be circular without worrying.

Rust pushes you to use arenas. This involves more ceremony than just using a direct reference, but it also means Rust pushes you to write code that computers can execute really efficiently.

I mentioned performance a number of times. But what about premature optimization? The great irony of this quote is that it comes from a paper where the author, Knuth, argues in favor of keeping the goto statement around, as it's essential for writing efficient software.

Industry observers note that rust lets you know what you pay for. Reference counting? Dynamic dispatch? You can do it, but it's going to be visible in your code. Rust also often lets you know when you don't want to pay for it: just look at tower middleware and despair about all the generic types and type constraints that get piled onto a relatively simple abstraction.

Sources indicate that when you have these tools available, need to develop newly introduced wisdom about tradeoffs that never seemed to matter. If you write Python code you're not too worried about hash tables being a performance bottle neck, but in Rust code they certainly can be. You can get lost along the way into hyper optimization land. Often you need to just get go 8. Many patterns that are just plain readable Rust code anyway happen to also be friendly to the CPU executing it.

Sources indicate that but Rust overwhelming you with details you may not want to think about is not the whole story, because performance is not just quantitative: if your code can truly be more performance, it can access new qualities. When you can write code that uses no memory and no CPU time 9, it changes how you think. It changes what's possible.

Sometimes the quality of performance is obvious: if you write numerical code, or a simulation, of course you don't want to wait for the answer. Being able to do many computations really fast is key to making AI possible.

Industry observers note that but it's more subtle that that: modern computers are really powerful, and ridicously fast, and we generally ignore that and just throw more resources at our problems. There are good reasons why this happens. But if we open our eyes a little, there are new architectural possibilities we can explore.

While the power of macros were the biggest language surprise, I think this is the biggest shift in my thinking: access to performance unlocks possibilities I hadn't considered before. Take my experiment Colchis: a library can store vast amounts of JSON in memory, while retaining full access, even indexed access (I still hope to add jsonpath one day!), to JSON data. Before Rust, this was a possibility that wasn't even on my radar.

Rust made me a better programmer because I can make the computer do more with less, opening up new areas of opportunity.

Sources indicate that rust is one of the most difficult programming languages I've learned -- and thus one of the languages that changed me the most. There's a simple part of Rust that isn't much harder to manage than any language, and in some cases may actually make your life easier -- enums, declarative type-driven frameworks, and the excellent dev tooling come to mind. Even arenas are fundamentally not that difficult to understand. The complexity is in unlearning some habits and learning newly introduced ones. And then there's a more challenging complex Rust, mostly, but not always under the surface, there when you need it.

According to recent reports, rust expands the reach of what I can build. That's what makes me happy I went on this journey. 10.

AI agents write a lot of code. They know the programming language, so do you need to know it? Does the language still affect the developer? If you share my belief it's good to look at the code, then it helps if you understand the code you're reading. I also think it's never been more crucial to think about how the systems you use affect the way you think and behave.

If you don't know what a struct is, just call it a class in your head, and you're good.

You have them in many languages but in impoverished forms, like true/false, or C's enum.

If you're going to do static type checking anyway for the guarantees it brings, perhaps use a language designed around it (enums!) that also gives you performance benefits?

Does AI truly understand? Do you want to have a philosophical debate? What do we mean by understand? Natural language is inherently stretchable.

Recent findings suggest that not impossible. I've seen it. People can do it if they really try, and it still makes life harder; it makes it much harder to test. But at least it's more obvious and more difficult to do.

Clone and own all the stuff! Which incidentally can also lead to more contiguous memory layouts...

No memory and no CPU time is an exaggeration, but little Rust programs sometimes feel that way.

Sources indicate that AI development is shifting all the tradeoffs in software development - they're not gone, but they have shifted. The AI can write Rust, even if you don't know it. But I trust plenty of contexts remain where my Rust experience plus AI leads to a better outcome than AI by itself.

#321. Launch HN: Axonnic (YC F26) – Sleeves that track fingers and estimate force

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 19m • 📚 Deep Dive (3864 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ycombinator

Launch HN: Axonnic (YC F26) – Sleeves that track fingers and estimate force

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 19 min read (3864 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ycombinator

⏱️ ~19 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We’re Arsh and Max, founders of Axonnic (https://axonnic.com).
  • We’re Arsh and Max, founders of Axonnic (https://axonnic.com).
  • Sources indicate that here’s a demo video: https://youtube.com/shorts/xBrocTc9cfAWe’ve found that electromyography (EMG) is a much better way to train robots than by video alone because video only captures movement, not muscle activity or the effort behind the movement.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that hi HN! We’re Arsh and Max, founders of Axonnic (https://axonnic.com). We’ve developed a forearm sleeve that reads muscle activity to decode finger movements and estimate fingertip force, while leaving the hands bare. It’s used to record human movement and generate training data for dextrous robots.Here’s a demo video: https://youtube.com/shorts/xBrocTc9cfAWe’ve found that electromyography (EMG) is a much better way to train robots than by video alone because video only captures movement, not muscle activity or the effort behind the movement. A useful signal can be present even when the hand barely moves; just maintaining a grip involves muscle activation. The subtle muscle movements that can barely be picked up in video are the most crucial details for activities like sewing and delicate assembly.The sleeve has 64 channels of surface electromyography, or EMG. Electrodes on the skin detect electrical activity from muscles in the forearm. We distribute sensors across the forearm so as to not overfit to one muscle group. We synchronize EMG with hand tracking to train a model that predicts finger joint angles, then we run the decoder solely from EMG, adding in fingertip force estimates that have been calibrated from finger presses on force sensors.When the user takes the sleeve off then puts it back on again, the electrode positions change, so we run tests over separate wearings. In one case, we ran a 215-second recording, four days after training, without any recalibration, and compared the results with Apple Vision Pro hand tracking. The result was just 6.9° error across 20 joint angles. We’ve published the measurements and evaluation details here: https://axonnic.com/benchmarks.We faced many challenges doing recordings in factories, including wireless interference and unreliable off-the-shelf hardware. This led to some bad recordings and the need to repeat data collection. For that reason, we’re developing our own electronics that use a wired PCB design that will eliminate interference and timing inconsistencies.Axonnic grew out of Max's EMG research at Oxford. We looked at using the technology for computer control, then we thought a more promising use-case was in capturing the effort involved in skilled manual tasks. This technology could be described as a computer to human interface. Where computers gain insight and learn from human skills. Sewing particularly stood out because the material deforms and the operator is constantly adjusting grip and tension.Maxim has an Oxford MBiol and conducted research on high-density surface EMG. He previously built internal tools at Skyscanner and worked at Voxblock across PCB development and supply chain. Arsh studied medicine at Oxford and has research experience applying machine learning to medical imaging, alongside software and robotics projects. Together we have built the sleeve, decoding software and data-collection system and tested them in industrial settings.So far we have the tech being used to record sewing and other manual tasks at a European manufacturer, which signed an LOI for support with robotic implementation. We have also collected construction demonstrations involving electricians, plumbers and demolition work. These are pilot and data-collection examples. Separately, our public demos include controlling a Proception robotic hand from forearm EMG.If you’ve done any of your own trials for training robots for manual tasks, we’d love to hear about what tasks you were trying to train for and how the trials went. We’re happy to discuss the hardware, calibration and models here in the comments. Thanks!https://axonnic.com Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50522776 Points: 25 # Comments: 10.

We’ve found that electromyography (EMG) is a much better way to train robots than by video alone because video only captures movement, not muscle activity or the effort behind the movement. A useful signal can be present even when the hand barely moves; just maintaining a grip involves muscle activation. The subtle muscle movements that can barely be picked up in video are the most important details for activities like sewing and delicate assembly.The sleeve has 64 channels of surface electromyography, or EMG. Electrodes on the skin detect electrical activity from muscles in the forearm. We distribute sensors across the forearm so as to not overfit to one muscle group. We synchronize EMG with hand tracking to train a model that predicts finger joint angles, then we run the decoder solely from EMG, adding in fingertip force estimates that have been calibrated from finger presses on force sensors.When the user takes the sleeve off then puts it back on again, the electrode positions change, so we run tests over separate wearings. In one case, we ran a 215-second recording, four days after training, without any recalibration, and compared the results with Apple Vision Pro hand tracking. The result was just 6.9° error across 20 joint angles. We’ve published the measurements and evaluation details here: https://axonnic.com/benchmarks.We faced many challenges doing recordings in factories, including wireless interference and unreliable off-the-shelf hardware. This led to some bad recordings and the need to repeat data collection. For that reason, we’re developing our own electronics that use a wired PCB design that will eliminate interference and timing inconsistencies.Axonnic grew out of Max's EMG research at Oxford. #319. My Quest to push native Three.js quality match AAA Game Engines

📅 09 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2419 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ben3d

My Quest to push native Three.js quality match AAA Game Engines

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2419 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ben3d

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that part 2 picked a pipeline for indoor scenes: lightmaps, light probes and reflection probes, with SSR, SSGI and ambient occlusion on top.
  • It has been revealed that the pipeline has two parts.
  • Each frame then reads those caches and adds the screen-space work on top:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that part 2 picked a pipeline for indoor scenes: lightmaps, light probes and reflection probes, with SSR, SSGI and ambient occlusion on top. Here I measure Three.js against it one stage at a time: what the games require, what Three.js has, and what is missing.

It has been revealed that the pipeline has two parts. The setup fills three caches: lightmaps for static meshes, a light probe grid for moving objects, and reflection probes for each room.

Each frame then reads those caches and adds the screen-space work on top:.

The biggest remaining gaps are in the SSR, SSGI and BRDF rows: Hi-Z tracing and coverage for SSR, the same coverage for SSGI, and above all the pluggable indirect lighting that ties both cascades into the BRDF.

It has moved this fast because of the Three.js maintainers. Michael Herzog (@Mugen87) has reviewed most of these PRs, and more than once has reworked one into a better design that fits how Three.js as a whole is built, adjusting the renderer's internals to make room for it. mrdoob has expressed strong support for many of them. I am very lucky to have both.

It has been revealed that what the games require. SSR, GTAO and the denoisers run in screen space before lighting, so they need per-pixel depth, normals, roughness, metalness and motion vectors. A deferred engine also stores base color and emissive, because its lighting pass reads only the G-buffer. Three.js renders forward and its beauty pass reads those from the material, so the G-buffer fits in 16 bytes per pixel. Part 2 has the layout and the memory budget for the whole frame.

What Three.js has. WebGPURenderer already renders a G-buffer prepass with multiple render targets, and the SSR examples use it today:.

It has been revealed that what is missing. Normal precision. SSR is unforgiving of normal error: a ray reflected off a slightly wrong normal lands somewhere visibly wrong at the end of a long trace. With RGB8 normals, smooth curved surfaces snap to a limited set of directions, and their reflections show banding and clumping.

AAA G-buffers use octahedral encoding: fold the sphere of directions onto an octahedron, unfold it into a square, and store two coordinates. It is the most accurate of the encodings surveyed by Cigolle et al. for its size. PR #35480 adds packNormalToOctahedral() and unpackOctahedralToNormal():.

RG16 snorm is the target, with RG16F as the fallback.

Reflections from RGB8 normals (left) and octahedral RG16F normals (right).

Normal error: RGB8 (left) and octahedral RG16F (right).

Industry observers note that what the games require. Bounce light baked into lightmaps for everything that does not move, and a probe volume to light dynamic objects, ideally one that does not leak light through walls.

It has been revealed that what Three.js has. Every standard material takes a lightMap, and there is now a complete baking pipeline in the browser to make one; that is Part 4. For dynamic objects, LightProbeGrid places a grid of probes through a scene, each storing incoming light as L2 spherical harmonics, and lights each object from the probes around it (example).

It has been revealed that the grid's limit was how long a capture took. Profiling showed the bake was CPU-bound on submitting render passes, so the batched capture renders eight probes per pass with one array camera, and a resolution-12 grid dropped from 5.6 s to 1.2 s. Culling each draw against its own sub-camera doubled that again. The grid now bakes about eight times faster than it did at the start of September, fast enough to re-capture a few probes per frame, and supports multi-bounce light. Integrating the spherical harmonics exactly also cut their error from 2.4% to 0.08%.

Industry observers note that what is missing. Probes leak. A probe on one side of a wall can light an object on the other, so a dark room glows with the light of the bright room next door. DDGI solves this by storing, with each probe, the distance to the nearest surface in every direction, and ignoring probes that cannot see the point being lit. I have DDGI-style visibility weighting working as a draft PR. Testing visibility against all eight surrounding probes was costly, so the draft can use tetrahedral interpolation, which blends four:.

Two rooms with probe visibility weighting.

Recent findings suggest that what the games require. Lightmaps are too coarse for contact shadows, and they know nothing about dynamic objects. Games add screen-space occlusion on top, and Activision's GTAO is the standard. It also produces a bent normal, the average open direction, which gives specular occlusion (GTSO): a reflection pointing into a fold of the surface is occluded, one pointing out of the opening is not.

Sources indicate that horizon-based SSGI, which is what Three.js has, runs the same depth-buffer search as GTAO and gathers light along the way. With SSGI on, its pass supplies the occlusion and the bent normal, and GTAO runs only when SSGI is off.

Which light the occlusion applies to matters as much as how it is computed. Occlusion is a shared buffer, set with builtinAOContext, and each source decides whether to read it:.

Sources indicate that what Three.js has. GTAO already feeds the lighting through a context, which is the pattern the indirect lighting design in Part 5 extends:.

GTSO (left) and scalar specular occlusion (right).

Sources indicate that SSR has its own series, Fixing Three.js's Screen Space Reflections. This section is the summary.

According to recent reports, what the games require. Shipped engines agree on a recipe, set out with its sources in How Games Do Screen-Space Reflections, and What Three.js Does Instead. In a cascade, SSR has to:.

What Three.js has. SSRNode importance-samples the full GGX lobe with correct Fresnel, can validate and refine its hits, and its result is reprojected and accumulated over time. The trace is a fixed-step march with short rays. The three SSR examples find 98%, 82% and 46% of the hits within their own ray length, in 2 to 3 ms, and the denoiser fills the gaps from neighbouring pixels. The result is composited over the image, as in the SSR example:.

What is missing. All five requirements, each prototyped or in review except ray reuse.

Exact tracing. A Hi-Z pyramid is a mip chain where each texel stores the nearest depth of the four below it. The ray takes large steps through empty space at coarse levels and single-pixel steps near surfaces, so it finds every hit the depth buffer contains and has no maximum distance to tune. My implementation adds a HiZNode that builds the pyramid in a compute pass. Trace time at 1920×1080, against the fixed-step march raised to the same hit rate:.

That is still a ray for every pixel. Tracing at half resolution with a joint bilateral upsample is written, and ray reuse between pixels, as Frostbite does it, is still to build. Exact Screen-Space Reflections on a Budget has the full plan.

In a recent development, coverage. Today a ray that misses samples an environment map inside SSR: an equirectangular texture passed in as environmentNode, which cannot be the PMREM-filtered scene.environment, let alone a local probe. Adding SSR over the image also counts the environment reflection twice. In a cascade, SSR outputs one thing: radiance premultiplied by coverage, with coverage 1 for a hit, 0 for a miss, and fading toward the screen border. The environment input and the BRDF estimate leave the node. This is prototyped as part of Pluggable Indirect Lighting for Three.js.

Sources indicate that tracing the previous frame. SSR cannot be part of the lighting while it reads the lighting's output. DOOM's answer is to trace the current depth buffer but read colors from the previous frame: reproject each hit point into last frame's TRAA output and sample it there. A hit that fails the check against last frame's depth gets zero coverage. Last frame's image already contained last frame's reflections, so a mirror facing a mirror gains a bounce each frame. Previous-frame tracing is in review.

According to recent reports, the loop needs two rules. The image SSR reads must be linear HDR radiance, taken after TRAA but before tone mapping and bloom, or reflections pick up tone-mapped colors and bloom halos. And the fed-back radiance must be clamped, because each frame's reflections become the next frame's input and a single firefly compounds frame after frame.

Reflections with previous-frame feedback.

Denoising. Three.js has two reflection denoisers. The pair the SSR example runs, TemporalReprojectNode and RecurrentDenoiseNode, reads every black pixel as missing data and fills it from its neighbours. That hides the tracer's misses and leaves nothing for the probes to answer. zalo's SVGF-based DenoiseNode replaced the pair in the SSR example and was taken back out five days later. I traced the flicker that caused it to the missing coverage: at the edge of a reflection a hit and a miss were averaged as two samples of one signal, and the history kept resetting.

My ssr-coverage branch carries coverage through every stage of DenoiseNode and takes its statistics from covered samples only. Still to do are a two-lookup history, a history cap that follows roughness, and skipping mirrors and matte pixels. The denoiser filters incoming light and the material applies its BRDF afterwards, so it needs no albedo in the G-buffer and no demodulation step. How Games Denoise Reflections, and What Three.js Does Instead has the comparison and the blueprint.

According to recent reports, what the games require. Engines that use SSGI as part of their lighting put it in front of their baked light as the first stage of the diffuse cascade. That means SSGI has to output coverage, trace the previous frame's lit image, and accumulate over time at half resolution.

Industry observers note that what Three.js has. SSGINode is built on the visibility-bitmask approach of SSRT3, which extends GTAO's horizon search to gather light as well as occlusion. One search of 24 depth samples yields a GI texture and an AO texture, and it is much less noisy than a single random ray, because each sample accounts for a whole arc of directions. The SSGI example traces the current frame's beauty pass and composites over it.

The third option also follows moving objects, and demonstrates no visible artifacts in the test scenes.

It has been revealed that what the games require. Indoors, one environment map is wrong: walk from a red room into a blue corridor and the floor should reflect red, then blue. Every game in the survey, and Unreal's reflection captures, use local reflection probes: cubemaps captured inside each room, each with a box describing the volume it influences. Inside its box a probe is box-projected, which removes most of a cubemap's parallax error (Lagarde's write-up is the classic explanation). Where boxes overlap, probes blend.

In a recent development, what Three.js has. CubeCamera captures a cubemap, PMREMGenerator prefilters it, and getParallaxCorrectNormal() box-projects it, as the box-projected environment map example shows. That is one probe per material, set by hand.

Two rooms lit by three box-projected probes.

What the games require. The bounced light has to go through the material's BRDF, so Fresnel, roughness and metalness apply to it as they do to direct light. In a forward renderer the beauty pass needs two inputs:.

In a recent development, three.js renders forward, so SSR, SSGI and AO are computed before the beauty pass and each material reads them while it shades. Tracing the previous frame is what makes that order possible.

Sources indicate that what Three.js has. Indirect diffuse is mostly in place: lightMap, LightProbeGrid and scene.environment all feed it, and AO reaches it through builtinAOContext. Indirect specular comes only from scene.environment, or a material's own envMap.

What is missing. A way to plug a screen-space result, or a cascade of sources, into a material's indirect specular, the way AO is plugged into its diffuse. This is the biggest gap in the pipeline, and my proposed design is in Pluggable Indirect Lighting for Three.js.

Industry observers note that what the games require. Temporal anti-aliasing whose output can also be next frame's input to SSR and SSGI, so it has to stay sharp under motion and must not feed ghosts or fireflies back into the reflections. Every engine this series measures itself against also renders below the output resolution and reconstructs the difference over time: TSR in Unreal, FSR 2 in Godot, DLSS and FSR in Cyberpunk 2077.

Industry observers note that what Three.js has. A TRAA node with Halton jitter, motion-vector reprojection and variance clipping of the history, and TAAUNode, which follows Karis's temporal supersampling and FSR 2. The TAAU example shows it at a quarter of the pixels:.

TAAU takes TRAA's place as the last stage of the frame. Everything before it runs at the render resolution, its linear HDR output is what the next frame's SSR and SSGI read, and bloom and tone mapping run after it. At a scale of 0.5, the screen buffers at 1080p drop from about 157 MB to 81 MB.

Wider clipping at rest. Variance clipping stops ghosting by rejecting history that no longer matches the current frame, and it also rejects good history. TRAA tightens its clip box to 0.5σ under fast motion, but at rest the box was 1σ, tight enough to clip converged sub-pixel detail, so a still image never fully resolved and longer histories scored worse. A drafted change widens the box to 2σ at rest and adds a historyLength control. Against a supersampled reference:.

Sharper history. History sampled bilinearly blurs a little more every frame the camera moves. Catmull-Rom history sampling, a draft PR, keeps it sharp. Both refinements apply to TAAU as well.

It has been revealed that TAAU in the full pipeline. The example upscales a single scene pass. The pipeline has a prepass, half-resolution effects and a beauty pass that all have to agree on resolution and jitter, and none of that has been tried together yet. With TAAU at 0.5, half-resolution SSR and SSGI would run at a quarter of the output resolution on each axis, so it may be better to run them at the full render resolution and skip the bilateral upsample.

Sources indicate that texture mip bias. Rendering at half resolution makes the GPU pick blurrier texture mips than the output deserves. Temporal upscalers pair with a negative mip bias of about log2 of the resolution scale, and Three.js does not apply one yet.

  • Sources indicate that each recipient should confirm their address by clicking a link in a confirmation email.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Starting in November 2026, we are gradually rolling out a requirement for every sending IP to have a valid HELO, a reverse DNS (PTR) record, and a matching A record. Use the HELO checker below to see whether the DNS meets our best practices, and follow the guidelines to avoid being listed.

It has been revealed that guidance for senders, mail admins, and postmasters on meeting Spamhaus's sending requirements. All senders must meet these minimum email sending requirements to avoid being listed.

Sources indicate that each recipient should confirm their address by clicking a link in a confirmation email. If no confirmation is received, do not send email to that address. Purchased, rented and harvested lists are the most common source of spam trap hits, and hitting traps is one of the fastest routes to a listing. See section.

Publish forward-confirmed reverse DNS for every sending IP.

According to recent reports, every sending IP must have a reverse DNS entry pointing to a fully qualified domain name (FQDN). That hostname must, in turn, resolve back to the same sending IP address. This is known as forward-confirmed reverse DNS (FCrDNS). An IP with missing or mismatched reverse DNS is treated as suspicious and is one of the most common reasons for an IP to be considered for listing. See section.

Use a HELO/EHLO hostname that resolves to the sending IP.

According to recent reports, the hostname the server announces in the HELO/EHLO command must resolve to the IP it is connecting from, and must stay consistent across connections from that IP. Placeholder values, hosting-provider defaults, and hostnames that vary between connections are treated as signals of misconfiguration or compromise and can result in a listing. See section.

Meet the IPv6 allocation and reverse DNS minimum.

According to recent reports, if sending over IPv6, the sending address must fall within an allocation of /64 or larger (a /64 is the standard block size we recommend assigning), and that space must have valid reverse DNS. IPv6 ranges without reverse DNS or with allocations smaller than /64 are often misused by spammers. See section.

Authenticate mail with SPF, DKIM and DMARC.

Publish SPF and DMARC records for every sending domain, sign every outbound message with a signature, and align the DKIM sending domain with the domain in the message's RFC 5322 From address. Authentication is one of the signals that shapes reputation, so gaps here make a listing more likely when other signals are weak. See section.

Recent findings suggest that enter your sending IP to check its HELO and DNS setup against our guidelines. Results may not be available for all IPs and some queries might not provide results for internal policy reasons. You can also check the current HELO by sending an email to helocheck@abuseat.org.

All sending infrastructure must have the following DNS and mailserver configuration. Failure to do so can result in IPs being listed on the Email Spam IPs (CSS) or compromised IPs (XBL) zones.

In a recent development, ensure the sending IP address has a valid reverse DNS (rDNS) entry resolving to a fully qualified domain name (FQDN) for the sending IP address. Spamhaus will treat emails originating from IP addresses without rDNS as suspicious and this will be reflected in the IP's reputation, and receivers using Spamhaus data may subject it to additional filtering.

Ensure the rDNS hostname resolves to the connecting IP address via a corresponding forward DNS (A/AAAA) record.

Abusive actors often rely on the reputation of upstream DNS records to hide their identity. Instead, configure a branded reverse DNS to use the sender's own domain, to improve trust signals for the IP address.

Industry observers note that do not use generic or auto-generated rDNS entries for dedicated IPs that point to the hosting provider (e.g., static-203-0-113-25.hosting.example.net, 203.113.0.25.broadband.example.net, vps-25.dedicated.hosting.example.com etc). These can negatively impact reputation.

Do not use random dictionary words in the rDNS and make it identifiable to the sending infrastructure.

Use the Spamhaus DNS checker tool to check your rDNS configuration.

Ensure the hostname used in the HELO/EHLO command resolves to the sending IP address.

Sources indicate that maintain a consistent HELO value that resolves to the sending IP address. Multiple HELO values resolving to different IP addresses may indicate residential proxy and/or malware behaviour.

Where possible, ensure the HELO/EHLO hostname is consistent with the rDNS hostname.

Host a webpage on the domain of the HELO, that explains what the domain is for, or that redirects to the main brand domain.

Do not use placeholder values such as localhost or generic hostnames that point to the hosting organization/ISP as the HELO value.

Do not resolve HELO hostname to infrastructure that is not used for sending â this behaviour is associated with spoofing and misconfiguration.

Do not use generic or auto-generated names provided by the hosting provider, use the sender's own domain where possible.

Do not impersonate the HELO value of well-known mailbox providers like Gmail or Hotmail.

Enter an IP address into the Spamhaus DNS Checker at the top of this page, to check its HELO value. An email can also be sent to helocheck@abuseat.org to check the HELO being used.

According to recent reports, IPv6 customer allocations must be at least /64 and must have valid reverse DNS. The /64 minimum is consistent with IPv6 subnet architecture and RFC 6177's guidance that email senders should be able to obtain at least a /64. This is further discussed in M3AAWG best practices for IPv6 allocation.

Add routes for all IP space owned by the sender to reduce vulnerability to BGP hijacking, which can allow hackers to send email that appears to originate from the IP space.

Run dig -x to confirm reverse DNS is present. To confirm the space is actually routed, look the address up at bgp.he.net.

Make sure SPF is set up correctly for the domain used in the envelope sender (RFC 5321 MAIL FROM), and points to the sending infrastructure.

Use SRS (Sender Rewriting Scheme) to rewrite the envelope From (MAIL FROM) if mail is forwarded, so SPF can still be checked against the forwarding domain.

Do not allow freemail addresses such as gmail.com or hotmail.com as the 'Envelope FROM.'.

Do not use the NULL envelope sender <> for anything other than indirect out-of-band delivery reports, DSNs and MDNs.

Do not send bounce messages after accepting unwanted mail. Reject it during the SMTP transaction instead. Bounces sent to forged senders are known as backscatter, which is indirect spam and can severely harm reputation.

Run dig TXT and confirm an SPF record is returned and includes the sending IPs.

Audit DNS regularly and remove records for services, hosts and IP space that are no longer used, including CNAMEs, NS delegations, A records and SPF include: entries for former providers.

Do not leave records pointing to decommissioned hosts or former providers. Dangling records can be claimed by others and used to send mail that appears to come from the domain.

Do not use wildcard DNS records.

This article explains domain, hostname terminology and domain alignment in email. Also, use aboutmy.email to check for email configuration setup.

Run dig against the subdomains and look for CNAMEs that resolve to a provider that no longer serves the domain.

It has been revealed that authentication is how receiving mail servers verify that emails are authorized to send from the domain. Without SPF, DKIM, and DMARC properly configured, the domain is exposed to spoofing and phishing, and emails are more likely to be rejected or flagged by Spamhaus.

Publish an SPF TXT record in the domain's DNS zone file that specifies exactly which IPs and hosts are authorized to send email on the domain's behalf.

It has been revealed that ensure the sending IP is explicitly included in the SPF record. Email sent from IPs not included in SPF will not pass SPF checks.

Industry observers note that make sure both the HELO domain and the envelope From domain have a valid SPF record. Publish SPF records on this domain (which might be the infrastructure domain) and not the visible header From domain.

Sources indicate that keep the SPF record within the 10 DNS lookup limit (this includes all nested include: statements). Exceeding the limit returns a PermError, which is not a pass, so SPF cannot authenticate mail or satisfy DMARC alignment.

Keep the SPF record as narrow as possible. Only include the sending infrastructure actually in use.

Do not use overly permissive qualifiers like +all or broad include: ranges that authorise IP space not under the sender's control.

It has been revealed that do not leave include: statements for providers no longer used for sending. Audit the SPF and remove outdated vendors. Check for typos.

Avoid using SPF macros unless needed. They are expanded per message at evaluation time, which is costly and makes failures more likely.

Do not use a or mx mechanisms where ip4: or ip6: would work. Each one costs a DNS lookup against the limit of 10, while ip4: and ip6: cost none.

Run dig TXT , then count the mechanisms that trigger a DNS lookup â include, a, mx, ptr, exists and redirect â and confirm the total is 10 or fewer.

Ensure every outbound message carries a valid DKIM signature, using a minimum 1024-bit key length while 2048-bit is recommended.

Ensure that the d= domain on the DKIM signature matches the domain on the header From.

Rotate DKIM keys at least annually, or immediately if a key is suspected to be compromised.

Use a different d= domain for different mailstreams (for example, separate subdomains for transactional and marketing email), so that each mailstream builds its own reputation.

Run dig TXT ._domainkey. (the selector is set in the ESP's DKIM setup page) and confirm a DKIM key, starting v=DKIM1, is returned.

Publish a DMARC record with a policy defined for the sending domain.

Ensure the header From domain aligns with the DKIM signing domain (d=) so that DMARC alignment passes.

Set up a DMARC aggregate report address (rua=) from day one as this will help audit email sent from the domain.

Do not remain at p=none permanently. Starting with p=none is acceptable, but we recommend having an enforcement policy.

Run dig TXT _dmarc. and confirm a DMARC record, starting v=DMARC1, is returned.

Send email only to people who want to receive it. Once the technical infrastructure is in place, the next step is building a legitimate list of email addresses from people who have provided explicit permission to receive the email. Lack of permission is one of the most common reasons for being listed by Spamhaus.

Ensure all bulk email is ONLY sent to recipients that have Confirmed Opt-in (COI). Send a confirmation email requiring recipients to explicitly opt-in to verify their email address. This will prevent unwanted signups, bot signups and typo email addresses. If no opt-in is received, do not send email to that address.

Utilise available signals like bounce data, feedback loops, postmaster tools and engagement data to ensure the mailing list is up to date and email is sent to an engaged audience.

Keep a timestamped record of when and how permission was obtained.

Do not send emails to purchased, rented, or harvested lists, as these are the most common source of spam trap hits.

Permission is NOT transferable. Do not grant or assume permission retroactively or transfer it between organisations or domains.

Look for high bounce rates, low engagement and unusual sign-up patterns in the mailing platform.

Refer to the guidelines from M3AAWG for managing spamtraps, and follow the best practices outlined in our resources.

Implement a robust email sunset policy to help remove temporary email sign-ups and email addresses that no longer engage with email.

Do not attempt to identify or suppress a spam trap address. Audit the acquisition process to identify which list segment or collection method introduced the problem address, and remove that source entirely.

According to M3AAWG spam trap best practices, mailboxes that remain inactive for more than 12 months can be repurposed as spamtraps.

Sources indicate that how email is sent matters as much as what is sent. Warming the IP and domain, maintaining a consistent volume, using trusted links and domains within emails, and providing clear, legitimate ways to opt-out of emails will help improve overall deliverability.

HELO domains which DO NOT have a sending history will be subjected to additional filtering. Please read our best practices around IP/Domain warm-up.

Start sending slowly, and consistently for any IP address or domain that has not sent email in the past 90 days, before gradually increasing volume.

Domains which have been registered in the past 24 hours will be part of Spamhaus Zero Reputation Domains (ZRD) list.

Additionally, domains used for mailing within 30 days of registration will be treated suspiciously and we recommend following best practices for newly registered domains.

Treat any change in IP or HELO hostname as a new asset if no prior sending history is available, and apply the same warm-up process as used for a new IP or domain.

Begin with a few initial campaigns sent to the most engaged recipients to reduce the risk of hitting older invalid addresses. Maintaining a slow and consistent email volume will help build a strong sender reputation.

Do not use warm-up services that generate artificial traffic or simulate opens, clicks and replies. Using an engagement inflation service will result in the IP or domain being listed.

Infrastructure operated to inflate engagement or otherwise trick filters will be listed as a spam-enabling service.

Do not send inconsistent email volumes or trigger a sudden spike in sending, as this could negatively impact reputation.

Do not send to addresses which are old and unengaged while warming the IP or Domain.

Recent findings suggest that do not send the entire daily volume in a single burst at the top of the hour. Spread it across the day as spikes in mail volume can look suspicious.

Do not use more IPs than required to manage the mail volume as this can be perceived as snowshoe behaviour.

Plot the daily send volume for the IP or domain against the warm-up schedule and confirm it is increasing gradually, not spiking.

Keep the overall bounce rate below 5%.

Suppress hard bounces immediately.

Investigate and remove repeated soft bounces after a defined threshold; this is typically 3â5 consecutive bounces.

Avoid using email list validation as a source to clean spamtraps as it does not do so, and is not and never will be a replacement for permission.

Use HTTPS for all links, and only use links generated by the sender's own system.

Sources indicate that sign or validate tracking and redirect links so they cannot be altered to point elsewhere. This prevents malicious actors from abusing them as open redirects.

Industry observers note that do not use free or unbranded URL shorteners in the content of an email. URLs and/or domains used in the content of an email will affect the overall reputation of the sending domain.

The reputation of the IP and domain as seen by Spamhaus can be checked via our reputation checker.

Spamhaus looks at multiple signals before assigning a reputation score, and a strong negative signal can outweigh the absence of positive ones â so following all email best practices consistently is essential.

Factors that influence reputation include: the service provider, the IP neighbourhood, the infrastructure the IPs are associated with, the upstream networks that connect to internet backbones, and the IP or domain's history â when it was first seen, when it was last used, and how it was used.

Check the IP reputation and domain reputation regularly and do not wait for a delivery concern or listing to discover an issue.

It has been revealed that associate the domain with network providers and registrars that maintain a good reputation. The reputation of the hosting provider or registrar can be checked on our reputation statistics page.

Ensure newly registered domains are not used for at least 30 days from registration. The domain can be used for non-email purposes during this period, and establishing a web-presence prior to sending email will help improve the credibility of the domain.

Refer to our recommendations for best practices when using newly registered domains.

Recent findings suggest that do not use newly registered domains in SMTP as a FROM domain or a HELO domain unless the domain is properly warmed up. Similarly, using a newly registered domain in the content of the email can also look suspicious. The age of the domains used in the email can affect the overall sending reputation.

Do not use cousin domains for additional mailstreams or geographies for the same brand. Use sub-domains.

Do not hide WHOIS information for the root sending domain. The reputation of the upstream provider may be used for evaluating domain reputation. The reputation of the upstream provider can be checked in our Registrar reputation page.

Run the domain through the Reputation Checker to get more insights.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A widespread, yet short-lived, system outage at United Airlines on Monday delayed some outbound flights at US airports, the airline told CNN in a statement, coming on the heels of a rare FAA ground stop that caused massive disruption.

The outage lasted about 30 minutes, with fewer than 150 flights impacted, United Airlines spokesperson Leslie Scott told CNN.

United acknowledged the problem just before 5 p.m. ET, saying the technology outage was impacting departing flights, and an hour later the airline declared it had been resolved.

“While some flights were delayed, there was no impact on flights in progress, or on United Express flights,” United Airlines said in a statement.

During the incident, the FAA stated United was experiencing a technology outage on its end and that “it’s not an FAA equipment matter.”.

‘Working on floppy disks’: FAA has fielded years of warnings about old systems.

United said there is no indication that the outage was a cybersecurity-related issue.

The technology outage affected access to multiple applications used by flight crews, according to an internal firm alert obtained by CNN.

Recent findings suggest that the airline instructed pilots not to log out of several systems, warning they may be unable to sign back in. The affected applications included flight planning, weather briefing and crew management tools.

Pilots unable to access their flight plans were being directed to contact dispatchers to have the documents emailed to them.

The memo did not disclose the cause of the outage.

Air traffic control audio captured by ATC.com indicates the moment the outage occurred.

“Hey, we’re uh, still waiting on our final weights,” a pilot on United Flight 1728 in El Paso, heading to Denver, said to a controller. “We just contacted ops and apparently there’s a manufacturer-wide system outage on it so might be a while.”.

The controller responds back, “United 1728, roger, so you don’t have any idea when you think you’ll be able to leave?”.

“No ma’am,” the pilot responds.

It has been revealed that the industry had largely returned to normal operations after the nationwide ground stop was lifted just after 8 p.m. ET on Friday, though airlines have still worked to reposition planes, crews and luggage as they grappled with the weekend’s score of cancellations and delays.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy held a 45-minute news conference Saturday morning to address the FAA ground stop, and apologized to travelers as he said he was still working to determine what exactly went wrong.

With the busiest travel season ahead, how likely is it that another FAA ground stop happens?

Duffy told reporters that upgrade work on an old telecommunication system could be a cause for Friday’s nationwide ground stop.

In at least one remote FAA location, Duffy remarked contractor L3Harris was doing routine maintenance to switch telecommunication lines from an old copper wire to fiber, which he described as “straightforward” work that has been happening across the country for decades.

As United Airlines indicated for Monday’s system outage, Friday’s ground stop didn’t appear to have been caused by a cyber attack or any “nefarious” activity, Duffy stressed at the news conference.

In a recent development, “A lot of questions came in yesterday. ‘Was this a, a cyber attack? Did some foreign nation attack this network?’ And the answer to that is we don’t believe so,” Duffy mentioned.

This story has been updated with additional information.

How to Break into Security, Ptacek Edition (2012)
