Immich App Stops Uploading: The Server Must Match the Mobile App Version

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1038 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, the Immich mobile app on my phone stopped uploading photos.
  • View the complete homelab infrastructure source on GitHub.
  • It has been revealed that immich runs on my k3s cluster as immich-server, immich-ml, immich-redis and immich-postgres-0, with the photo library on an NFS export.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Originally published at woitzik.dev.

In a recent development, the Immich mobile app on my phone stopped uploading photos. Selecting photos and starting a backup did nothing. On the server side everything looked healthy: all four pods Running, storage with plenty of room, ingress answering 200, no errors in the log. The cause was on the phone. The app had auto-updated from 3.2.1 to 3.3.3, the server was still on v3.2.2, and the app quietly refuses to upload to a server older than itself. Bumping the server to v3.3.3 fixed it. It was also the second time this happened in a month.

View the complete homelab infrastructure source on GitHub.

It has been revealed that immich runs on my k3s cluster as immich-server, immich-ml, immich-redis and immich-postgres-0, with the photo library on an NFS export. The phone backs up over the home LAN. On 2026-10-18 I noticed that backups had stopped. No error dialog on the phone that pointed anywhere useful, and nothing on the server side that looked like a failure.

My first suspicion was infrastructure, because that is where things usually break in my setup: storage, the database, or the LAN ingress path.

I worked through the stack from the bottom:.

It has been revealed that every one of those checks was green, and none of them could explain the problem. A failing upload would leave a trace somewhere in that list. There was none, which meant the uploads were not failing. They were not happening.

The useful signal was in the server's own request log, once I stopped looking for errors and looked at which endpoints the phone actually called. The app was connected and busy:.

Sources indicate that authentication worked and sync worked. What was missing was POST /api/assets. The app never even tried to upload. Whatever was stopping it had to be on the client side, before any upload request was built.

The one call in that list that reads like a gate is /api/server/version. The app asks the server what version it is, every time.

It has been revealed that immich records the client build for every session in its Postgres database. The session table has an appVersion column, so I queried it:.

Industry observers note that the last 3.2.1 session dates from 2026-09-28. On 2026-10-18 the phone reported 3.3.3. The app store had updated it in the background. The server reported something older:.

In a recent development, app 3.3.3, server v3.2.2. The Immich mobile app refuses to sync or upload when the server is older than the app build. That guard lives entirely on the phone. The server never sees a rejected upload because the app never sends one, so every server-side health signal stays green while backups stop.

The reason the server was on v3.2.2 is PR #747, from 2026-09-17. Its title notes it all: "bump immich to v3.2.2 to match mobile app 3.2.1 sync requirement". Back then the app had jumped to 3.2.1 while the server was still on v3.1.0, with the same result: no uploads.

Industry observers note that right after #747 I added a Renovate rule (#748) so the server would never lag the app again. Immich had been in my "stateful, PR-only" group, the same group as databases and Vault, because Immich upgrades can carry database migrations. I moved the server and ML images out of that group into their own rule:.

That rule should have caught v3.3.3. It didn't, and I only found out why weeks later. My Renovate config uses minimumReleaseAge as a soak period, and that setting requires a release timestamp by default. Docker Hub publishes one. GHCR, where Immich lives, does not. So GHCR updates sat in "pending" forever and never became PRs. A debug run on 2026-11-10 listed about 20 of them, immich-server v3.3.6 among them. The fix (#1058) lets Docker updates without a timestamp skip the soak:.

Industry observers note that CI still has to pass, the stateful PR-only group still applies, and majors are never auto-merged. The v3.3.6 revision (#1060) landed the same day. If you run Renovate with minimumReleaseAge and pull images from anything other than Docker Hub, check whether your updates actually arrive.

The immediate fix was a manual bump of immich-server and immich-machine-learning to v3.3.3, pinned by digest, in kubernetes/apps/immich/immich.yml:.

The ML image (and its fix-cache-ownership init container, which uses the same image) moved to v3.3.3@sha256:73915f07... in the same commit. I left the Postgres image alone. v3.3.3 is a patch release with no database image change.

In a recent development, before applying it I took a pg_dump and stored it next to Immich's own daily dumps on the library volume. That dump is the real rollback path. Immich does not support downgrades, so reverting the image tag alone would not undo the upgrade once the server has run its migrations. A rollback means the old image plus the pre-upgrade database dump.

Once app and server versions matched, uploads resumed.

Sources indicate that this is not a one-off bug, so I recorded it as ADR-061 and as a known gotcha in the Immich README. The coupling is permanent: the phone updates itself whenever the store decides to, the server updates when I (or Renovate) decide to, and any gap where the app is newer means backups stop with no server-side error.

Industry observers note that the README entry states where to look: the app checks /api/server/version against its own build, and session.appVersion records what each client reports. That table is the fastest way to see which builds your users are running, without asking anyone to open the app's settings screen.

It also corrected something in my own documentation. In my operating model post I listed Immich among the apps with data migrations that stay PR-only. For the server and ML images that is no longer true: minor, patch and digest updates auto-merge, and only majors wait for me. The data migration risk is still real, which is why the pre-upgrade dump habit matters more now, not less.

The same pattern of a green status hiding a broken function came up in my health probe post: the checks I had were all real, they just measured something other than "can the phone upload a photo".

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev

Tech Report: A PDF table can keep every number and still break retrieval: an audit workflow

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (698 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that A table can survive PDF extraction with every number intact and still become misleading.
  • According to recent reports, this walkthrough uses KolmoPDF's PDF-to-Markdown converter and a small audit fixture to check that a table remains usable for retrieval.
  • Choose a document you have permission to upload.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that A table can survive PDF extraction with every number intact and still become misleading. If the column heading falls off a page or gets attached to the wrong row, a search result may return a plausible value with the wrong unit or reporting period.

According to recent reports, this walkthrough uses KolmoPDF's PDF-to-Markdown converter and a small audit fixture to check that a table remains usable for retrieval. The fixture is illustrative, not a claim about a particular conversion result.

Choose a document you have permission to upload. Find a table with a unit in its heading, a footnote, or rows that continue onto another page. Note its printed page number and PDF page number: front matter can make them different. Keep the original PDF so a reviewer can compare each result with the source.

For example, suppose the source has this table, with the final row on the following page:.

Industry observers note that an extracted row such as B | 95 | 2.1 is incomplete on its own. The values need the column names and units. If the source also qualifies those measurements in a footnote, the qualification belongs in the evidence a reader can inspect.

Open the converter, upload the PDF and convert it to Markdown. The service handles technical layouts including tables and formulas. Download the result and locate the table by its caption or a distinctive row label. Check the rendered Markdown and the raw text: a pipe character inside a cell, for example, can change how a Markdown table renders unless it is escaped.

Compare the output against the source:.

Sources indicate that A continuation page may produce a second table. If it lacks headings, add the original headings to that fragment before indexing, but keep a pointer to the pages from which its rows came. Do not assume two nearby tables are one continuation: compare captions, column structure and surrounding text first. When the source is ambiguous, send it for review instead of joining rows automatically.

Industry observers note that the converter processes documents online. Use an approved workflow for confidential material, and check the output on representative pages before processing a larger collection. Complex layouts and scans deserve particular attention; conversion does not guarantee that every cell or formula will be correct.

A chunk containing only B | 95 | 2.1 asks the retrieval system to infer too much. A more useful chunk repeats the table title, heading and relevant note:.

Sources indicate that keep provenance in metadata as well as in text if your retrieval system supports it. Use the actual PDF page range for each chunk, including both pages when a row or note crosses a boundary. If the Markdown export does not supply reliable page references, capture them during review rather than assigning a guessed page.

Recent findings suggest that repeat headings when splitting a long table into row groups. Keep a footnote with every group it qualifies, and retain the original full table for inspection. For a table with multi-level headings, flatten the heading path explicitly, for example Latency / p95 (ms), after checking that it describes the original cell.

Recent findings suggest that write a few questions with answers you can verify in the PDF. For the fixture above, ask for system B's latency and its unit, then ask which system has an error rate of 0.9%. Check the retrieved chunk before looking at the generated answer. It should contain the correct row, the heading and the source reference. Also ask a question for a value absent from the table; the system should have an opportunity to say the evidence is missing rather than filling in a number.

According to recent reports, record the failures by type: extraction, table reconstruction, chunking, retrieval or answer generation. A correct answer with the wrong citation still needs work. Re-run the same questions after a parser or chunking change, and include examples from scanned pages and multi-page tables if those appear in your documents.

In a recent development, the KolmoPDF product overview covers the available output types. For a separate check on mixed scanned and text pages, see page-level OCR routing.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Attackers' AI agents have been hunting for weak spots in internet-exposed AI apps such as LiteLLM, One API, and Dify to steal the AI provider keys stored inside, according to the agents' own records.

The records, which Amazon's threat intelligence team captured with decoy servers, describe stolen keys being used to run the AI models that powered the search for more keys.

Recent findings suggest that the team said this week that it cannot verify the outcomes reported by the agents. It has moderate confidence that the agents ran on ARTEX, an open-source AI tool for penetration testing.

The records include a playbook of known entry points for each targeted product. It lists default administrator credentials such as LiteLLM's default master key, unfinished installs that an outsider could take over, and known flaws in Langflow and RAGFlow.

In a separate case reported this week, Cloudflare's incident responders saw ARTEX gain access to a compromised API token that had been used for CI/CD. The token had no IP restrictions or rate limiting, and the activity that followed included 400 database dump requests in an hour. The organization has not said whether those requests returned any data.

It has been revealed that an operator gives ARTEX a target and a goal, and a planner agent splits the goal into tasks for worker agents that run security tools. To decide each next step, the agents send their work to a large language model (LLM).

It has been revealed that the decoy servers, part of a network called MadPot, posed as popular LLM services. From October 3 to late last week, the agents sent it requests that often carried a campaign's full history, including the operators' instructions and the agents' reported findings.

Those captured agent records describe work done on systems MadPot does not watch. "Amazon Threat Intelligence did not observe that activity as it happened and cannot verify the outcomes the agents reported, but the records show what the actors were pursuing," the team said.

The team assessed, with moderate confidence, that the operators were separate China-linked groups, citing Simplified Chinese prompts and China time zone settings, among other evidence.

Industry observers note that in the main campaign, the agents looked for internet-exposed AI apps, extracted the provider keys stored inside, verified that the keys worked, and added them to a shared pool. They focused on apps that hold keys for many providers, because one weak admin page there can expose many accounts.

Targets named in the records include LLM gateways and proxies such as One API, Newly introduced API, Veloera, Sub2API and LiteLLM, and AI app builders such as Dify, FastGPT, Langflow, RAGFlow, Open WebUI, LobeChat and Ollama.

The playbook also covers management and provider settings endpoints that need no login, an authentication bypass through the isCliRequest header in One API family systems, and server-side request forgery (SSRF) through URL-fetch features to reach cloud metadata services. Other entries cover secrets left in client-side JavaScript, source maps, debug routes and environment files.

When the agents found cloud credentials, they targeted managed services that host AI models, secret stores, and application identities, prioritizing premium AI models over general cloud access.

To find leaked keys, the agents used internet scanning services and certificate transparency logs, and searched GitHub repositories and event archives, npm and PyPI packages, container image layers, notebooks, model-hosting spaces, paste sites, and Telegram channels.

According to recent reports, the records cover hundreds of targets across AI app platforms and other systems. The team notified AWS customers who may have been affected.

Microsoft reported last week that attackers were using agentic AI tools such as ARTEX for GitHub secret hunting, looking for exposed credentials that included API keys for AI inference.

On August 26, the company described an earlier RAGFlow attack, in which a hidden hook captured AI provider keys as users entered them, and a compromise of a LiteLLM gateway that exposed provider keys.

In its RAGFlow case study, the firm had only low confidence about which flaw, if any, let the attackers run code. It did not link those attacks to ARTEX.

The decoy records also describe a second campaign in which agents attempted to bypass identity checks at two cryptocurrency exchanges using deepfakes.

In a recent development, one verification vendor's server rejected the live deepfake video on every attempt the agents made to record it. The team did not say whether the forged photos of ID documents that the agents also fabricated passed document checks.

Over the past eight weeks, Cloudflare's incident responders were called into multiple investigations involving ARTEX and tools built from it.

In more than one incident, an attacker gained access to a customer's environment with a major cloud provider and moved directly into the customer's Cloudflare account. The common root cause was static CI/CD tokens that never expired, granting broad access across the customer's cloud setup, according to the company.

In the ARTEX case, the compromised token was an account-level API token. The compromise most likely came through a third-party cloud provider, according to the manufacturer's incident findings. How the token was first stolen has not been disclosed.

Latest Worker scripts with names such as artex-*, artex-pgrecon-*, artex-pgw-* and artex-do-* appeared in the account, each name matching a different task. The activity ran at more than 69 requests per minute across several parts of the account. It included attempts to establish persistence and validate session tokens for other third-party apps.

Much of this activity was lightly guided by a human operator, the company believes. Whether any attempt at persistence worked has not been disclosed.

Over three days this week, more than 50 families of AI penetration testing frameworks tried to scan the firm's customers, and the IP addresses seen running such frameworks now number in the thousands.

It has been revealed that the FBI remarked in a FLASH alert this week that a range of attackers have used ARTEX since at least August against organizations in many sectors around the world. The alert summarizes 11 earlier reports and describes no new incident.

ARTEX's developer made its GitHub repository unavailable on October 8 after reports of abuse, but community forks, archived copies, and a commercial version called ARTEX PRO keep it available.

The alert's examples include an earlier campaign against South Korean financial institutions that stole personal information on about 67,000 people, and the ConnectWise compromise.

Sources indicate that "None of the techniques in these campaigns were fresh. What AI agents change is the speed and persistence of the attacker," Amazon's threat intelligence team mentioned. The agents succeeded where basic security was missing, including default or hard-coded credentials, keys left in code and public files, interfaces and inference endpoints without authentication, and unpatched software.

The team recommends treating AI apps, model gateways, and inference endpoints like other production systems, assuming that exposed secrets will be found promptly, and watching for misuse through unexpected spending or unusual usage.

#261. GitHub Copilot Credit Cliff: What the Reset Changed

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (783 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev

GitHub Copilot Credit Cliff: What the Reset Changed

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (783 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that on June 1, 2026, GitHub Copilot rewired how every enterprise pays for it.
  • To smooth the transition, GitHub handed out enhanced credit allowances through September 1, 2026.
  • That was the trap, and it is worth naming plainly because this kind of increase does not announce itself.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that on June 1, 2026, GitHub Copilot rewired how every enterprise pays for it. Premium request units are gone. In their place is a token-metered system called GitHub AI Credits, where one credit equals one cent and every interaction draws down a monthly pool based on the input, output, and cached tokens each model consumes. Seat prices did not move, Business is still 19 dollars per user per month and Enterprise still 39, but the way usage is billed changed completely. The transition shipped with a promotional allowance, and that allowance ran through September 1, 2026.

To smooth the transition, GitHub handed out enhanced credit allowances through September 1, 2026. During that window, Business seats included 3,000 credits per user each month and Enterprise seats included 7,000. On September 2 those allowances snapped back to their standard levels: 1,900 credits for Business and 3,900 for Enterprise, which is where they sit today. No contract changed. No developer behaviour changed. But the usage covered by the seat you already pay for fell by roughly 37 percent on Business and 44 percent on Enterprise, overnight.

That was the trap, and it is worth naming plainly because this kind of increase does not announce itself. Teams spent the summer letting developers use Copilot freely, calibrated their sense of normal against the promotional pool, and then received a materially larger invoice for the exact same work. Because overages bill at published rates once the pool is exhausted, the gap never demonstrated up as a price increase. It showed up as consumption the team was always doing, now landing above the line.

Consider an Enterprise organization with 500 developers whose typical usage ran near the promotional ceiling of 7,000 credits per user. Before September that sat inside the included pool, so the marginal cost was zero. Now only 3,900 credits per user are included. The remaining 3,100 credits become overage: at one cent each, that is 31 dollars per user per month, or 15,500 dollars a month across the team, about 186,000 dollars a year in fresh spend that nobody approved, because nobody bought anything. Your real number depends on your actual token mix; treat this as the shape of the risk, not a quote.

The mechanics reward a particular kind of discipline. Credits are pooled at the billing entity rather than stranded per seat, so one developer's light month can offset another's heavy sprint, but only if someone is watching the pool as a whole. Unused credits do not carry over: the pool resets to the full monthly amount at 00:00:00 UTC on the first day of each calendar month, and whatever is left is forfeited. Code completions and Next Edit suggestions remain free and never touch credits, so the drawdown is driven almost entirely by chat, agents, and premium-model calls. The heavier the model and the longer the context, the faster the pool empties.

According to recent reports, the first full billing cycle under the standard allowances has now closed, which makes the impact measurable rather than hypothetical. Three checks matter most.

Copilot was not an outlier. Cursor moved to usage-based, API-pegged billing and then began retiring its flat Auto rate in August 2026, and the industry has converged on the same model: seats get you in the door, tokens determine the bill. That is a structural change in how AI coding tools are priced, and it quietly moves the cost-control burden onto the buyer. Fixed per-seat pricing let finance forecast with a spreadsheet. Token-metered pricing means the bill is now a function of developer behaviour nobody can see in a contract, and it only reconciles thirty days after the fact, when the invoice arrives.

That is the gap Olumia was built to close. We connect to the AI coding assistants your teams use, such as Copilot, Cursor, Claude, OpenAI and more, through read-only APIs and forecast spend before it lands, so a change like the September credit reset is something you model in advance instead of explaining afterwards. The method itself is vendor-agnostic and written up in how to track AI code assistant spend across every vendor.

Recent findings suggest that the promotional window closed on September 1. Included Copilot credits fell by up to 44 percent, seat prices did not move, and the difference now lands as overage on work teams were already doing. Pull the first full cycle under the standard allowances, compare it against a summer baseline, and decide the overage policy deliberately rather than discovering it on the next invoice. The question was never whether the reset was coming. It is whether it reveals up in your forecast before it shows up in your invoice.

Show HN: Coral – Open-source gateway where agents write their own tools

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1090 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Github

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Coral is an open-source, self-hosted gateway that sits between your agents and the systems they work on.
  • In a recent development, in this example, an agent posts unreviewed PRs to Slack for the first time.
  • Industry observers note that control what agents can do, not just what they can reach.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Coral is an open-source, self-hosted gateway that sits between your agents and the systems they work on. Agents call tools by writing short TypeScript programs, and save the ones that work as custom tools to reuse. Coral checks every call against your policy before it adds credentials and forwards the call.

Quickstart · Download · Demo video.

In a recent development, in this example, an agent posts unreviewed PRs to Slack for the first time. The agent searches for the GitHub and Slack tools and writes code that calls them. It isn't allowed to post to Slack without approval, so the user approves the post. The agent then saves its code as a custom tool. The next day, the agent runs the same task by calling that custom tool.

Industry observers note that control what agents can do, not just what they can reach. Most MCP gateways decide only which tools an agent can see. That is all or nothing: if an agent can call update_record, it can update any record in any way the tool allows. A custom tool is code, so it can hold the rule that Allow and Block cannot: closeStaleTicket changes one field, only on tickets with no activity for 30 days. You set Allow, Ask, or Block on the custom tool like any other tool, and Coral still checks every provider call inside it against your policy.

Less duplicated agent work. Agents start every task from scratch. They re-read tool schemas, retry failed calls, and spend tokens rewriting code for steps they got right yesterday. With Coral, agents save the code that worked as custom tools they call again in one step, and workspace owners can share them with the whole team.

Coral is used by thousands of developers at more than 450 companies for safer, more efficient agent work in customer support, SecOps, business intelligence, SRE, and more.

Add a provider. A provider is one service your agents can use, such as GitHub or Linear. Pick one from the catalog, or bring your own OpenAPI document or MCP server. By default, tools that read data run right away and everything else needs your approval. See Add a provider.

Connect your agent. Copy your workspace's MCP URL from the Coral UI and add it to your MCP client:.

For Cursor, VS Code, OpenCode, and other clients, see Connect an MCP client.

Sources indicate that ask a question. Ask your agent something that uses that provider, such as "What are my open pull requests?".

It has been revealed that we started Coral while building an AI SRE. To investigate an incident, the agent had to connect the dots across an ocean of telemetry and undocumented relationships between internal and external systems. It needed broad permissions and a lot of tokens, and it started from scratch the next time.

According to recent reports, we built Coral so that the agent remembers the route. Once a task succeeds, the agent saves the steps that worked as a custom tool. Next time, it finds that tool in the same search as provider tools such as Datadog and Slack. It started with SRE, and teams now use Coral for agent work across the organization:.

From one developer's laptop to an enterprise cloud, Coral fits your stack:.

In a recent development, agents write programs. Coral builds on code mode, and adds custom tools, policy controls, and managed identities. To use tools, an agent writes a short TypeScript program. One program can call several tools, filter the results, and return only what the task needs. Less raw data passes through the model's context.

According to recent reports, coral runs them on rails. Each program runs in a fresh V8 isolate with no network access, no credentials, and no imports. Coral checks every tool call against your workspace policy, then adds the credentials and forwards the call to the provider. A policy can also require a person to approve the call. Every run is attributed to the person or agent that started it.

The agent sends Coral programs through the exec tool. A program calls coral.search to find the tools the agent can use and read their TypeScript signatures. Then the agent sends a program that does the work. This one finds open pull requests that have no reviewer and posts them to Slack:.

Sources indicate that if posting to Slack needs approval, the run pauses there until you approve it. Only the pull request numbers go back to the agent, not the full GitHub response. The run happens on the Coral server, not in your agent, so it carries on even if the agent disconnects.

Recent findings suggest that what works becomes a custom tool. When a program succeeds, the agent saves it as a private tool and calls it next time in one step as coral.private.({ ... }). Agents find custom tools in the same search as provider tools, and reuse or edit them instead of starting over. A workspace owner can publish a private tool as a shared tool under coral.shared, so everyone in the workspace can call it.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News Airbnb Introduces CASTLE for Training Natural Language Search Models with Synthetic Data.

Nov 16, 2026 2 min read.

It has been revealed that airbnb researchers have introduced CASTLE, a framework designed to address the cold-start problem in natural language search. The approach uses de-identified booking sessions and large language models (LLMs) to jointly generate synthetic search queries and relevance labels, enabling model training before sufficient real search traffic is available.

Natural language search allows guests to describe their preferences in everyday language, such as "romantic cabin near skiing" or "pet-friendly beach house that sleeps eight", rather than relying exclusively on predefined filters. Training such systems presents two challenges: generating queries that reflect actual user behavior and determining which property listings are relevant to each query.

It has been revealed that previous approaches, including InPars and Promptagator, address query generation and relevance labeling as separate tasks. They use LLMs to generate queries from documents or examples, followed by additional model-based judgments to assign relevance labels. According to the researchers, this separation can introduce additional sources of error and differences between synthetic and real-user query distributions.

It has been revealed that CASTLE uses contrastive listing pairs derived from de-identified booking sessions. When a guest books a property after viewing several alternatives, the selected listing becomes a positive example, while another viewed but unbooked property serves as a negative example. An LLM is then prompted to generate a query that matches the positive listing but not the negative one. This allows relevance labels to be established through the construction process rather than through a separate evaluation step.

In a recent development, the framework combines three query-generation strategies: template-based prompts, few-shot prompts using approximately 500 seed queries collected through targeted user research, and attribute-grounded prompts focusing on distinguishing listing characteristics. A variety mechanism also encourages variation in query length and phrasing.

For listing pairs without sufficient booking history, including newly listed properties, CASTLE uses a Virtual Judge, an LLM-based evaluator that assigns relevance labels to additional query-listing pairs. The researchers also developed CASTLE-R, a variant intended for production environments where real search traffic has started to accumulate.

According to recent reports, in the evaluation, CASTLE achieved a Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence of 1.01 against real-user query distributions, compared with 9.33 for the best baseline, Promptagator. This represents a 9.2-fold reduction in divergence. At the attribute-type level, CASTLE achieved a KL divergence of 0.08, compared with 0.09 for manually curated survey seed queries. Source: Medium Blog.

It has been revealed that the researchers also conducted a human evaluation in which three independent subject matter experts reviewed 200 sampled triplets. Agreement with CASTLE's relevance assignments ranged from 91% to 93% across the three evaluators.

The evaluation methodology also prompted discussion on LinkedIn. Mark Tsai, an AI Engineer specializing in LLM fine-tuning and evaluation, raised a question about potential overlap between training and evaluation data:.

Recent findings suggest that do the training and evaluation splits keep seed templates and listing IDs disjoint? For synthetic triplets, I’d compare a random split with that stricter split, then evaluate on untouched real queries. It would help separate learning reusable intent–attribute matches from recognizing familiar templates or properties.

Recent findings suggest that wendy Ran Wei, the article's author, responded that the team evaluated the model on untouched real queries and implemented leakage guardrails when constructing evaluation sets. She also clarified that the paper does not report a controlled comparison between random splits and stricter splits with disjoint seed templates and listing IDs, identifying this as a possible direction for further investigation.

The full paper is available on arXiv.

Presented by: David Iparraguirre - Senior Product Marketing Manager at Datadog, and Jessica Yang - Product Manager at Datadog.

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A financially motivated threat activity cluster tracked as REF3364 has been attributed to a Linux-focused cryptocurrency mining operation that tampers with the readings used to detect high GPU workloads.
  • Central to the intrusion is a toolkit called SANSAR, a Rust-based orchestrator that receives commands over the TOR anonymity network to manage CPU and GPU miners.
  • "The threat actor also deployed a kernel rootkit to hide selected processes and files, an NVIDIA Management Library (NVML) wrapper to falsify GPU readings, and a separate backdoor named netns," Elastic Security Labs stated in a report published last week.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A financially motivated threat activity cluster tracked as REF3364 has been attributed to a Linux-focused cryptocurrency mining operation that tampers with the readings used to detect high GPU workloads.

Central to the intrusion is a toolkit called SANSAR, a Rust-based orchestrator that receives commands over the TOR anonymity network to manage CPU and GPU miners. The activity was observed in late October 2026.

"The threat actor also deployed a kernel rootkit to hide selected processes and files, an NVIDIA Management Library (NVML) wrapper to falsify GPU readings, and a separate backdoor named netns," Elastic Security Labs stated in a report published last week.

"This backdoor retrieves its C2 [command-and-control] address from an Ethereum smart contract before connecting to the server directly.".

Sources indicate that in the attack chain documented by the manufacturer, initial access is stated to have been achieved via an exposed Ray job agent, allowing the threat actor to execute commands. This includes jobs running the NVIDIA System Management Interface (nvidia-smi) to capture and exfiltrate the GPU inventory to an external server.

Subsequently, the attacker submitted a Python reverse shell job that connected to a remote listener, after which an SSH key was added to that account's authorized_keys file to establish persistent access.

"After obtaining root, the actor staged the toolkit under /opt/vadi_, built the acpi_thermal_mgr kernel module through Dynamic Kernel Module Support (DKMS) and added an initramfs loader," security researcher Salim Bitam remarked.

In a recent development, "An initramfs is a temporary root file system loaded into RAM during early boot, before Linux switches to its normal root filesystem. The module and loader are stored in the boot image on disk, so the rootkit can load again when the host boots with that image.".

According to recent reports, the installation also delivers a modified NVML wrapper that filters process information and changes GPU telemetry to evade detection. Specifically, the altered wrapper hooks NVML calls used by monitoring tools such as nvidia-smi to report GPU utilization as 0%. In addition, temperature and power readings are substituted with random values between 36 to 46 degree Celsius (96.8 to 114.8 degree Fahrenheit) and 100 to 200 watts.

Also delivered are the following payloads -.

Sources indicate that once introduced, SANSAR first performs an anti-debugging check by reading the value of TracerPid and exits if it's non-zero. TracerPid indicates the Process ID (PID) of the process currently tracing or debugging the target process.

It then reaches out to an onion service ("efxisnqldelyr5ra25oqfrsut54b34g26e7zrsiuupsoekjof2gho2id[.]onion") for C2 communication via Arti, receiving commands, collecting host and GPU information, and fetching the miner status. The main responsibility of SANSAR is to supervise the mining process and launch the appropriate miner executable based on the miner type (i.e., CPU or GPU) specified in the C2 response message.

The "acpi_thermal_mgr.ko" kernel rootkit, on the other hand, uses Function Tracer (ftrace) to conceal cryptomining activity on Linux systems by hiding processes, files, and socket entries.

It achieves this by intercepting system calls to directory listings, file access, and process termination signals, removing matching records or blocking requests for those hidden processes and files by returning the message "No such file or directory" or "No such process.".

It has been revealed that the other main component of the operation is the netns backdoor that's registered as a systemd service. It's used to retrieve a controller IPv4 address by sending requests to an embedded contract (0x43eb291f56688c63c93e8a93c4591fc997cf6349) and then sets up a plain TCP connection to that address on port 8080 to open a reverse-shell connection to the specified host and port in the C2 response.

It's not clear who is behind the operation, but Elastic noted it found Turkish language comments in the rootkit's source code.

"Organizations expanding GPU infrastructure for AI and LLM workloads should check who can submit jobs and whether GPU monitoring libraries have been modified, as cryptojacking can divert compute capacity from legitimate workloads and increase operating costs," Elastic remarked.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recall brings candidate pages in: anything that might be what you mean.
  • According to recent reports, spotRecall, my private on-device browser recall extension, has spent several releases building recall.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Filler words, bookmark titles, and look-alike rows — three quiet refinements that make the first screen of results more useful.

Good search is a balance between two forces.

Recall brings candidate pages in: anything that might be what you mean. Precision puts them in order, so the page you actually want sits at the top of a short list. Most search improvements push on one side, and the best ones arrive in pairs.

According to recent reports, spotRecall, my private on-device browser recall extension, has spent several releases building recall. It matches any query word rather than requiring all of them, so long Japanese and Chinese phrases still find pages. It expands prefixes, so gar finds gardening. And since 1.1.0 it seeds the index with your bookmarks and open tabs, so useful pages are searchable from the first minute, before they have been revisited and captured.

Version 1.3.1 adds the precision side of each of those choices. None of the changes is large, and the first one below was the largest measured step in the release.

Industry observers note that when SpotRecall imports a bookmark, at first it knows only the title and URL. The page content arrives later, the next time you visit. Until then, the record is title-only.

Recent findings suggest that titles are short, and keyword search rewards a term that makes up a large share of a short field. SpotRecall's BM25 index also weights the title three times higher than body text, which is the right choice for captured pages. Together, this means a title-only record that shares a single word with the query can score surprisingly well.

One example from the test suite: the query 门牌 网购 (doorplates, online shopping) against a bookmark titled 买手网，您身边的网购帮手 (a shopping-assistant site). The bookmark shares 网购, but it is not about doorplates at all.

1.3.1 adds a query-dependent prior for title-only records:.

The phrase "of some query variant" matters. Each query is also searched in translation, so a bookmark that fully matches the English or Japanese version of the query keeps its full weight. A genuine title match — Japan Patent Office for the query japan patent — is untouched. Only the partial overlaps step back, letting pages that actually contain your words come first.

This was the largest measured step in the release. On 54 real queries against a 1,088-record backup, MRR rose from 0.809 to 0.828. In a worst-case simulation, where every backfilled bookmark also receives SpotRecall's bookmark boost as it would in a bookmark-heavy profile, MRR rose from 0.787 to 0.826.

The three behaviours are pinned by tests: a stray single-term match is down-weighted, a full match on any variant keeps full weight, and records with captured content are never touched.

Matching any query word is what makes SpotRecall forgiving with natural-language and CJK queries. It also means every word in the query brings its own candidates.

Most words bring useful ones. A few bring almost everything. The Chinese particle 的, the Japanese particle の, and English words like of and the appear in a large share of all pages. With prefix matching on top, of would even expand into office and offer.

1.3.1 handles this on the query side, with two small rules:.

It has been revealed that the index itself is unchanged; pages keep every word. Only the query is focused, which keeps candidate lists centered on content words without affecting what can be found.

In a recent development, spotRecall already collapses duplicate content. URLs are normalized (tracking and session parameters removed), and pages with an identical content hash are shown once, keeping the best-ranked copy.

Sources indicate that some pages are near-identical rather than identical. Two sessions of the same chat app, for example, can differ by a few characters in the captured body, which gives them different hashes. On screen they look the same: same title, same preview text.

1.3.1 adds a second, display-level pass. Rows that share both their title and their visible snippet are shown once:.

Industry observers note that this follows how consumers judge duplicates — by what they can see. As with the content hash, an empty key never merges anything: a record without a title always keeps its own row.

Every recall feature in SpotRecall now has a precision counterpart:.

Recent findings suggest that looking at the list this way also gives a design rule for the future. Whenever a change widens what search can find, ask what tells the ranking which of the latest candidates are worth showing first.

Sources indicate that search quality is often won in small, explainable signals: which words carry meaning, how much a title-only match really proves, and what a user will perceive as a duplicate. Each rule here is a few lines of code, a test, and a measurement — and together they made the first screen of results noticeably more focused.

SpotRecall 1.3.1 is rolling out on the Chrome Web Store and Microsoft Edge Add-ons, with release notes in 21 languages.

According to recent reports, spotRecall is open source under AGPL-3.0. spotrecall.com · source on GitHub · install from the Chrome Web Store.

One of the US Army soldiers that survived an Iranian strike that hit a makeshift operations center in Kuwait and killed six has submitted a whistleblower complaint alleging that the Pentagon did not listen to concerns about the lack of proper protection for troops, according to a copy of the disclosure obtained by CNN.

The complaint, submitted last week to the House and Senate Armed Services committees and first reported by CBS, comes as Democrats are poised to launch wide-ranging investigations into the Trump administration and its handling of the Iran war when they take control of Congress in January.

CNN has reached out to the congressional committees and the Pentagon for comment.

Army Maj. Stephen Ramsbottom outlined why he submitted the report in an exclusive interview with CBS’ Norah O’Donnell on “60 Minutes” that aired Sunday, describing the March 1 attack as a “tactical failure” by “the Army, our leadership, and myself.”.

Recent findings suggest that “We just did not initiative this well, and this needs to be a lesson that we learn,” he noted. He added that some people described the operations center as a “trailer park.”.

It has been revealed that the six US Army Reserve soldiers killed in the strike at Kuwait’s Shuaiba port were the first US service members killed in the US’ war with Iran. Dozens, including Ramsbottom, were wounded.

While senior Pentagon officials said at the time that the building was fortified, a source familiar with the site previously told CNN it was only surrounded by concrete barriers that would provide protection from car bombs but had nothing to shield it from drones or missiles. CNN also previously reported that the attack came quickly and with no warning or sirens to alert troops to evacuate or get into a bunker, according to a source familiar with the situation.

Ramsbottom stated he brought up the lack of protection from aerial attacks to his superiors in various meetings and was told: “We don’t have to worry about protection.” Military leaders later said that they were going to try to get a counter-drone system sent to the site, but “it never arrived at Shuaiba and we don’t know if it was ever even ordered to or requested,” he said.

Industry observers note that the installation did not have a physician or a fixed aid station when the drone strike happened, according to the whistleblower report. There was only one ambulance at the site.

According to recent reports, ramsbottom has made similar claims in interviews with multiple outlets since the attack. In an interview with CNN affiliate KOAA news in April, he recalled that while the facility had protections for “legacy threats” like mortar fire or car bombs, it wasn’t prepared for modern drone warfare.

In a recent development, “It was well-fortified for that type of thinking from pre-Russian invasion of Ukraine. It was a pretty well fortified base. But it wasn’t well prepared for the type of fight that we’re getting into,” he told the news station.

At a press conference after the attack in March, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth mentioned that the US has “incredible air defenders,” but acknowledged that “one” projectile had made it through in the attack.

“Every once in a while you might have one — unfortunately, we call it a squirter — that makes its way through. And in that particular case, it happened to hit a tactical operation center that was, that was fortified, but it — these are powerful weapons,” he remarked.

Sen. Richard Blumenthal, who sits on the House Armed Services Committee and is the top Democrat on the Senate’s Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, has asked Hegseth to appear in a classified briefing to answer questions and provide “all force protection assessments” about the facility at the Shuaiba port.

It has been revealed that uber’s Legal Redlining Agent has reduced average contract review time by more than 20%, with 91% accuracy in AI-generated decisions, according to the organization. Integrated into Microsoft Word, the agent analyzes proposed contract changes, assesses legal risks, and recommends policy-aligned responses using retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), historical lawyer feedback, and deterministic rules. Lawyers retain responsibility for reviewing and approving its recommendations.

The agent identifies edits proposed by external parties, interprets their intent, compares changes with legal policies, and suggests whether to accept, reject, or modify clauses. It also generates comments explaining recommendations and flags changes requiring closer scrutiny. Uber began developing the first generation in early 2024 and piloted it with its Legal team in 2025.

High-level workflow of the Legal Redlining Add-in / Agent (Source: Uber Blog Post).

Sources indicate that an initial RAG implementation retrieved relevant sections from legal playbooks to guide language model responses. However, the system struggled with semantic retrieval accuracy, negotiation tone, and scenarios not covered by existing examples. Uber subsequently added a feedback loop that captures lawyers’ decisions, reasoning, and final edited text.

Recent findings suggest that this change allowed the agent to retrieve examples of how similar clauses had been handled rather than relying only on whether a previous recommendation was accepted or rejected. At runtime, similarity search and metadata filtering narrow thousands of historical interactions to approximately 20 candidates. A second language model-based filtering stage evaluates their relevance. Exponential decay weighting, with a configurable half-life currently set to 365 days, prioritizes recent decisions while retaining older examples. The implementation also gives domain experts control over language and negotiation style.

Uber Engineering framed the challenge in its LinkedIn post:.

How can AI help streamline repetitive contract review while keeping lawyers in control?

Industry observers note that the legal team defines the desired tone and style, while engineers maintain the prompt structure and application workflow. The architecture combines a React and TypeScript Word add-in with a Python backend orchestrated through LangGraph. Parallel workflow nodes handle intent detection, risk assessment, and policy lookup. OpenSearch stores vectorized legal rules and historical feedback, while Redis maintains session state for follow-up questions.

Legal Redlining Agent system architecture (Source: Uber Blog Post).

According to recent reports, A deterministic rules engine enforces non-negotiable legal requirements and overrides model recommendations when a matching rule applies. Language models handle tasks requiring contextual interpretation, including clause recommendations and negotiation tone. A final verification step checks generated responses against retrieved rules.

Uber is also exploring agentic harnesses, including Claude Code and OpenCode, alongside skills to structure and automate workflows across its agentic AI efforts. The team looks to investigate legal ontologies and knowledge graphs to represent legal concepts and relationships, providing a semantic foundation for more consistent interpretation and reasoning.

In a recent development, say the AI change touches Opportunity. A few lines of pandas give you a review agenda:.

Paste those three tables into the ticket. The question for the reviewer is no longer "does this Flow work?". It is "what else will run when this record is saved?". A clean-looking change can collide with an old rule, loop with another flow, or overwrite a field that a batch still expects to find empty.

Sources indicate that managed package automation will also appear in some of these queries. If you only want what your team owns, filter out rows whose name or namespace you do not maintain. Keep the managed ones in a second list: you cannot edit them, but they can still fire after your change and surprise you.

None of this proves the change is wrong. It does justify waiting a day when:.

The model accelerates the draft. The list tells you where to look. Someone with experience still decides when that draft is not ready.

#246. Retadup Worm Resurfaces 7 Years After Takedown to Spread CoffeeLoader Malware

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (590 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thehackernews

Retadup Worm Resurfaces 7 Years After Takedown to Spread CoffeeLoader Malware

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (590 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thehackernews

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of a new variant of CoffeeLoader, a malware designed to deliver additional payloads to infected machines.
  • "On launch, the NSIS-based installer executable dropped a file named '7z.dll' into a temporary directory and ran it through rundll32.exe," Kaspersky mentioned in an analysis published today.
  • Sources indicate that "The '7z.dll' file was a patched version of the original library of the popular 7-Zip archiver.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of a new variant of CoffeeLoader, a malware designed to deliver additional payloads to infected machines.

"On launch, the NSIS-based installer executable dropped a file named '7z.dll' into a temporary directory and ran it through rundll32.exe," Kaspersky mentioned in an analysis published today.

Sources indicate that "The '7z.dll' file was a patched version of the original library of the popular 7-Zip archiver. Part of its code had been replaced with malicious self-decrypting shellcode that turned out to be a fresh version of the Armoury packer.".

CoffeeLoader was first documented by Zscaler ThreatLabz in March 2025, detailing its use of the Armoury packer to resist analysis and ultimately run Rhadamanthys shellcode. The malware is assessed to share source code similarities with another loader family tracked as SmokeLoader.

Malware packed with Armory uses file names like "ArmouryAIOSDK.dll" and "ArmouryA.dll," with the packer hijacking some of the original Armoury Crate functionality with self-decrypting shellcode.

It has been revealed that notably, the shellcode extracts code that executes a decryption routine on a system's GPU by making use of the OpenCL library. The end goal is to install CoffeeLoader, establish persistence, and execute it by injecting it into a newly created "dllhost.exe" process.

In a recent development, the latest version of the packer continues to use the GPU, but replaces OpenCL with the OpenGL library. In addition, the latest version of the packer delivers intermediate shellcode instead of a DLL. This shellcode serves as a downloader responsible for fetching the main CoffeeLoader malware.

"To establish persistence, the Trojan copies '7z.dll' to subfolders of %PROGRAMDATA% or %LOCALAPPDATA%," Kaspersky mentioned. "The Run registry key is used for autorun. The subfolder, library, and registry value are named with eight hexadecimal digits generated from system volume information.".

"To protect itself, the downloader creates a registry key that prevents the user from disabling autorun through Task Manager.".

Once persistence is successful, the malware rolls out one of the legitimate processes (e.g., "dllhost.exe," "WerFault.exe," "svchost.exe," "OpenWith.exe," or "AtBroker.exe") and then injects itself into it, after which the malware shellcode is downloaded from a hard-coded command-and-control (C2) server.

The shellcode then decrypts and runs the CoffeeLoader payload. It supports the same three commands to run the next-stage malware from the C2 server -.

As for how CoffeeLoader is distributed, it takes place via Retadup, a Windows computer worm that was disrupted by French law enforcement authorities in August 2019. The malware, which spreads via infected USB drives, has been used to drop additional payloads like cryptocurrency miners, the Stop ransomware, and the Arkei password stealer.

"Two years ago, someone began re-registering the domain names that Retadup had used as C2 servers and using them to issue commands to download third-party malware," Kaspersky said. "At first, this was the SmokeLoader downloader packed using the 32-bit version of Armoury, but in early 2025, the same servers started serving CoffeeLoader.".

Recent findings suggest that it remains unclear whether the worm's author or some other threat actor was instrumental in bringing the C2 servers back online. Kaspersky stated it blocked around 15,000 systems from being infected with the resurrected version of the worm, most of them located in Peru, Angola, Russia, and Bolivia.

In a recent development, quemia es una aplicación educativa creada en Cuba para aprender química jugando. No es un libro digital ni una lista de fórmulas: es un juego completo en el que cada nivel te enseña un tema, cada ejercicio te explica por qué, y cada error se convierte en una oportunidad de repasar y entender.

Aprender. Niveles por temas, para avanzar paso a paso como en un juego: cada nivel superado es un tema entendido, no una página más del libro. Se aprende jugando, no memorizando.

Tabla periódica. Una tabla periódica interactiva para consultar y aprender los elementos en cualquier momento, sin buscar en un libro ni depender de internet.

Repaso de errores. Todo lo que se falla queda guardado para repasarlo después, así ningún error se queda sin entender y nada se olvida por no practicarlo.

Duelos. Duelos en línea con amigos, para retarse y aprender compitiendo, con la emoción de jugar contra alguien de verdad.

Y además: rachas diarias, recordatorios de estudio y el progreso guardado, para que el hábito de estudiar se mantenga día a día; modo claro y oscuro; y funciona sin conexión, así que se puede estudiar en el aula, en el transporte o en casa, con o sin internet.

Está pensada para estudiantes universitarios de química pura, pero también para cualquier persona que quiera entender la materia paso a paso, desde cero y a su propio ritmo.

Quemia no viene a sustituir al profesor ni al libro: viene a poner la práctica en manos del estudiante, todos los días y en cualquier lugar. Cuando aprender se convierte en un juego, el estudiante no estudia porque tiene que estudiar: estudia porque quiere seguir jugando, seguir subiendo de nivel y seguir ganando. Y ahí es donde cambia la educación: no en la tecnología, sino en las ganas de aprender.

Industry observers note that JEP 547, Lazy Constants (Fourth Preview), has been elevated from Candidate to Proposed to Target for JDK 28. This JEP proposes a fourth preview, with no changes, after three rounds of preview delivered in the upcoming release of JDK 27 and JDK 26 through JDK 25. Formerly known as Stable Values and Computed Constants, this feature introduces the concept of computed constants, defined as immutable value holders that are initialized at most once. This offers the performance and safety benefits of final fields, while offering greater flexibility as to the timing of initialization. The name change from Stable Values to Lazy Constants with the release of JDK 26, better captures the intent of a high-level use case. The review is expected to conclude on Wednesday, November 18, 2026.

Recent findings suggest that build 24 of the JDK 28 early-access builds was made available this past week featuring updates from Build 23 that include fixes for various challenges. More details on this release may be found in the release notes.

For JDK 28, developers are encouraged to report bugs via the Java Bug Database.

The second release candidate of Spring AI 2.1.0 delivers fresh features such as: a new DecisionModel API, anchored by the DecisionModel interface, that returns the probability of different outcomes instead of generated text based on yes/no answers, questions about text or a set of fields; and a new similaritySearch(float [], SearchRequest) method, added to the VectorStoreRetriever interface to complement the corresponding overloaded methods, to search with a user's embeddings in more vector stores. Further details on this release may be found in the release notes.

According to recent reports, the second release candidate of Spring Boot 4.2.0 ships with bug fixes, documentation improvements, dependency upgrades and new features such as: support for reading the value defined in a X-Forwarded-Prefix HTTP header in a WebFlux application on Reactor Netty when the server.forward-headers-strategy property is set to native; and a database assigned to the spring.data.redis.database property is now properly applied to master/replica connections if a value is assigned to the spring.data.redis.masterreplica.nodes property. More details on this release may be found in the release notes and this wiki page.

The Spring for Apache Pulsar team has confirmed that the project is moving as a subproject within Apache Pulsar at the Apache Software Foundation to "foster even deeper integration and collaboration with the broader Pulsar community." As stated in the blog post:.

Bringing this integration directly into the Apache Pulsar project allows the community to streamline development, accelerate feature support, and ensure long-term alignment with the evolution of Apache Pulsar.

Spring for Apache Pulsar 2.0.8, released in October 2026, was the final release under the auspices of the Spring ecosystem.

According to recent reports, the fourth milestone release of GlassFish 9.0.0 provides bug fixes, documentation improvements, dependency upgrades and new features such as: implementation of the Jakarta Persistence 4.0.0-M7 specification with EclipseLink 6.0.0-M1; a move of the Sun Theme module out of the out of the external GlassFish Woodstock Components repository into its own module in GlassFish so that Sun Theme and the Admin Console can be modified together; and an update to versions 1.2.0-M2 and 2.0.0-M1 of Eclipse JNoSQL. Further details on this release may be found in the release notes.

It has been revealed that beehive Lab, makers of TornadoVM, has released version 3.0 of jitLLM, a JVM-native LLM inference and serving engine, delivers notable changes such as: 1.43 times faster startup with GraalVM Native Image; an up to 9.3 times faster prefill phase; and a more efficient reading of model weights by eliminating the copy from the mapped GGUF file into a Apple Metal buffer. More details on this release may be found in the release notes.

The first release candidate of Hibernate ORM 8.0.0 ships with notable changes such as: an implementation of the Jakarta Persistence 4.0.0-M7 and Jakarta Data 1.1.0-M4 specifications (the latter via Hibernate Data Repositories); and support for coordination of graph-based flushing that builds a dependency graph for pending entity and collection mutations. These versions are compatible with Hibernate ORM 8.0.0.CR1. More details on these releases may be found in the release notes for version 5.1.0.CR1 and version 5.0.0.CR1.

Further details on this release may be found in the release notes.

The first rolling release of JReleaser 2.0.0-SNAPSHOT provides a latest feature in which the -a and -d short option flags, for their respective corresponding --assembly and --download long versions, were removed from the CLI due to the lack of short option flags for the --changelog and --announce flags. Further details on this release may be found in the release notes.

More details on these releases may be found in the release notes for version 2.4.0 and version 2.3.0.

#243. Six Unpatched Danfoss Refrigeration Controller Flaws Could Allow Remote Takeover Without Login

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (998 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thehackernews

Six Unpatched Danfoss Refrigeration Controller Flaws Could Allow Remote Takeover Without Login

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (998 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thehackernews

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Six flaws in Danfoss AK-SM800A refrigeration controllers could let a remote attacker take over a controller without logging in, Dutch security consultancy Midnight Blue stated earlier this week.
  • No patch is available, and the researchers say the newest firmware, version 5.4.0, does not fix the flaws.
  • Government cybersecurity agencies in Belgium, Ireland and Germany told operators this week to take the controllers' management interfaces off the internet.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Six flaws in Danfoss AK-SM800A refrigeration controllers could let a remote attacker take over a controller without logging in, Dutch security consultancy Midnight Blue stated earlier this week.

No patch is available, and the researchers say the newest firmware, version 5.4.0, does not fix the flaws.

Government cybersecurity agencies in Belgium, Ireland and Germany told operators this week to take the controllers' management interfaces off the internet.

It has been revealed that for a controller left on the internet, updating the firmware, changing default passwords or turning on Strict mode is not enough on its own, the Belgian and Irish agencies remarked. Strict mode is a login protection that requires encrypted connections and session tokens, but one of the six flaws is in the gateway that enforces it.

Industry observers note that the AK-SM800A runs a store's fridges and freezers, and maintenance firms can manage it remotely. Such controllers were targeted in attacks in France starting October 11, and in a second wave across Europe that began last week. The attacks caused unwanted defrost cycles and destroyed stock.

Germany's federal IT security agency, the BSI, says in a security notice that the AK-SM800A was involved in earlier incidents in which refrigeration units in several countries were tampered with.

The agency has no information about any exploitation of the six latest flaws, and neither other agencies nor researchers link the flaws to those incidents.

The researchers examined firmware version 5.3.2, then the newest, and say every version up to and including it is affected.

No CVE identifiers have been assigned. The researchers are keeping technical details private while they work on disclosure with Danfoss, the Danish organization that makes the controllers.

According to recent reports, the vendor lists software package 5.4.0, dated November, as its newest release for the AK-SM800A. Its 5.4.0 readme and November patch guide cover upgrade steps, and the guide adds a stricter password rule. Neither mentions a fix for any vulnerability.

In a follow-up statement carried by trade publication Cooling Post, the researchers said 5.4.0 does not patch the flaws: "It's not really possible either because according to the file timestamp this firmware was likely built on October 29, before the second wave of cyber attacks and well before our vulnerability reports.".

Industry observers note that the German agency first said in a press release this week that 5.4.0 was not affected. Later the same day, it changed that in a corrected statement: it cannot rule out for now that 5.4.0 is affected.

The vendor's advisory page lists no advisory for the six flaws as of today, and no date for a fix has been published.

Midnight Blue researcher Carlo Meijer found the six flaws in less than an hour of manual review, using firmware the vendor offers for download, and described them in a technical write-up.

Industry observers note that five of the flaws are in web request handlers that do not require a login, inside a program that runs as root. Through one of them, the researchers ran code as root on older firmware, version 3.3.0, and they found the same bugs in 5.3.2.

In a recent development, strict mode closes almost all of the controller's web attack surface to people who have not logged in, including the flaw used in that demonstration. The sixth flaw is in the gateway that enforces Strict mode, a separate program that blocks every request except the login until a user has logged in.

When the researchers ran firmware 5.3.2 in an emulator with Strict mode on, that flaw crashed the gateway. The crash could be turned into code execution with more work, the researchers say, and the gateway lacks basic exploit defenses such as stack canaries.

With code running as root, an attacker could change the controller's settings, start defrost cycles and hide that activity from its logs.

Recent findings suggest that the controllers do not use secure boot, the researchers found, so an attacker could plant code that survives a factory reset and a firmware revision. An attacker could also make a controller unusable until it is replaced.

The researchers say the code almost certainly holds more flaws like these, and they call patching flaws one by one or turning on Strict mode "a misallocation of scarce security and personnel resources.".

Removing internet exposure must not wait for a patch, and it is needed even where firmware is current and Strict mode is on, the Centre for Cybersecurity Belgium indicates.

The Belgian advisory and a similar Irish advisory recommend these steps:.

The German agency adds that anyone who suspects a compromise should change all credentials and check that equipment connected to the controller works properly.

Before cutting off the data a controller sends to its refrigeration service company, operators should check contract and insurance terms, the Belgian advisory claims. They should also set up protected remote access so that monitoring can continue.

Danfoss's own upgrade guide indicates the AK-SM800A should not be directly reachable from the public internet, adding: “This recommendation applies to all software versions, including those with Strict Mode enabled.”.

Ireland's National Cyber Security Centre also advises running the latest supported firmware, changing default passwords and turning on Strict mode, but claims operators should not rely on those steps alone.

Danfoss told Cooling Post on October 12 that most units hit in France were either older models that no longer receive updates or current AK-SM800A units running outdated firmware.

Recent findings suggest that the vendor fixed earlier flaws in the AK-SM800A in 2023 and 2025, including login bypass and command injection bugs. Version 5.3.2, which the researchers examined, is newer than all of those fixes.

Recent findings suggest that CVE-2026-107145 affects the Roundcube twofactor_gauthenticator plugin. It is fixed by commit 4640889d71a25391d8814de826f39416bf3db08d, which changes authentication state handling rather than a single string comparison. A deployment check that only confirms a file exists is weak.

Industry observers note that the fix must be tested through the login flow and the AJAX verification endpoint. It must also be tested after a failed logout, through a reverse proxy, and across repeated logins. Each check maps to a documented failure that existed before the commit.

Record the plugin source, package version, and commit used to build each web node. The advisory lists all versions before 4640889 as vulnerable. If the plugin is copied into a container, confirm the running image digest and the file content in that image, not just the repository branch.

Industry observers note that compare local modifications with the upstream change. The fixed code adds a persistent state file under log_dir, options for twofactor_lockout_delays, twofactor_lockout, and twofactor_trusted_proxies, and a server-side session teardown. A local fork that lacks one of these changes may need further review.

Sources indicate that start with a test account. Submit an incorrect six-digit code through the normal login path. Observe the configured delay and confirm that another request is rejected as blocked for the remaining interval. Then start a new login sequence and verify that the failure level has not been reset by the previous logout.

According to recent reports, repeat the test through the AJAX check-code route. The upstream change requires an explicit secret for the self-test path and avoids returning a success or failure verdict while the account and source are blocked. Do not use a production account or a real user's TOTP secret for the test.

Check that a successful code clears the counter and that the counter expires after the configured window. Verify that the state file is written to the intended Roundcube log_dir with restrictive permissions.

It has been revealed that send a direct request with a forged Client-IP or X-Forwarded-For value. The application should use the real TCP peer and must not grant whitelist access from the forged value. When testing through an approved proxy, confirm that its address is included in twofactor_trusted_proxies and that the resolver chooses the expected client hop.

Industry observers note that run one test with an untrusted proxy and one with the intended proxy. Do not add broad ranges to make a test pass. A secure configuration should fail closed when the peer or forwarded chain is not recognized.

Recent findings suggest that the vulnerability requires the password and network access to the login path. The CNA record gives CVSS 4.0 a 6.3 Medium score. A test plan should include account recovery, session revocation, and mailbox rule review, not just the positive login case.

Recent findings suggest that if the patch cannot be installed immediately, use gateway request limits and restrict access while maintaining an explicit remediation deadline. Review logs for repeated second-factor failures and unexpected whitelist bypasses. The advisory did not report public exploitation, but local telemetry determines whether suspicious activity occurred.

The same advisory covers CVE-2026-107146 for session persistence and CVE-2026-107147 for spoofed client headers. A test that covers only CVE-2026-107145 can miss behavior that the commit also changes. Include all three checks in change verification and retain the evidence with the deployment record.

According to recent reports, zoomEye Search app="Roundcube" returned 61,971 product-fingerprint matches. The exact CVE Filter returned 0. This is useful for finding candidate deployments, but not for proving plugin installation or patch status. Verification starts with owned assets and their actual build artifacts.

According to recent reports, if you used AND.CO's free strategy, you probably found out the way most people did: you went to send an invoice and the app wasn't there. Fiverr's help center gave March 1, 2026 as the date Fiverr Workspace (the product AND.CO had become) was discontinued, with data export open until that day and browser-only. Type and.co into a browser today and you're passed to workspace.fiverr.com and then on to the ordinary Fiverr homepage. We checked that redirect again on November 16.

In a recent development, A lot of the internet hasn't noticed. On November 11 we went through 33 pages that rank for "best invoicing software for freelancers" and similar searches, and 16 of them still recommended AND.CO as a live product, several as the top free pick. So if you're reading a roundup that sends you there, that's why the button goes nowhere useful.

Most of the migration guides you'll find are written by paid tools, which is fair enough. They want the AND.CO Pro customers. This page is for the other group: people who were on the free blueprint, had a client or two, and don't want a monthly bill for sending a handful of invoices.

Sources indicate that it's easy to remember AND.CO as "the free invoicing app", but its free tier did more than invoices, and it had one hard limit. Fiverr's own pricing listing on G2 (last updated by the vendor in October 2024) describes the free plan as working with one client "for as long as you like", and lists, among other things:.

Pro, at $18 a month billed annually or $24 monthly, lifted the one-client cap and added editable contracts and your own branding.

According to recent reports, that list matters, because no single free replacement covers all of it. The honest move is to split it in two.

This is where we'd point you at Mini Accountant, which is ours, so weigh that accordingly. Every feature in it is free on iPhone, iPad, Android and the web. The optional Pro subscription only removes the "Powered by Mini Accountant" line from your invoices and reports.

Against the AND.CO free list, it covers:.

It also runs from places AND.CO never did: a Telegram bot, and an MCP server, so you can ask Claude or Cursor to draft an invoice or log an expense.

For someone who used AND.CO's free plan with one or two clients, that's most of the day-to-day.

Here's what Mini Accountant does not do, so you can decide before you move anything:.

It has been revealed that if proposals and time tracking were the reason you used AND.CO, a free invoicing app is the wrong replacement and you'll be happier with an all-in-one tool, paid or not. If invoices, payments and a year-end report were the reason, you don't need to pay for a suite to get them back.

Industry observers note that you can't export from AND.CO any more. Fiverr's export window closed with the service. If you did download your invoices before March, keep the PDFs as they are; they're your record of what was billed, and you don't need to re-key old invoices into a newly introduced app to stay in order.

In a recent development, what's worth re-entering is anything still open: invoices issued but not fully paid, and the clients behind them. Create the customer with the currency you bill them in, recreate the open invoice with its original number and date, and record whatever part has already been paid. From then on, the reports pick up where AND.CO left off.

Sources indicate that and if you're the person maintaining one of those roundups that still lists AND.CO: the link goes to Fiverr's homepage now. Your readers would probably like to know.

Emacs Is My Browser
